Summary and Conclusions The Homeric poems contain around a dozen stories that have more or less close parallels in international oral tradition. The source stories show considerable variety, ranging from such complex and widely- distributed folktales as The Ogre Blinded to such simple and sparsely- distributed legends as The Petrified Ship. Most of them occur in the Orfyssey, for which reason the poem has been called a Märchenepos, a folktale epic, but this appellation is misleading. It would be truer to say that about a dozen stories in Homer have parallels in interna­ tional oral tradition, most of them occurring in the Orfyssey, where they are told as legends. HOMER AND THE FOLKTALE 461 Homer is not likely to have been the inventor of the stories in question, nor do the international analogues derive from the Homeric poems; rather, the Greek bards drew independently upon the inter­ national tradition. The only story in which the question of priority has been much debated is that of The Ogre Blinded, and

even here nearly all scholars have concluded that Homer’s version is not the source of the international tale but an independent realization of it. In a couple cases, the ancient and modem parallels may not be genetically related at all. There is a tendency in studies of folk narratives in Homer to link the notions folktale and fabulous. This coupling can have undesirable consequences because realistic stories may be excluded from the consideration of traditional stories in Homer and because Homer’s use of folktales may be regarded as being the same as his employ­ ment of the fantastic, which it properly is not, since not all folktales contain fabulous motifs and not all fabulous motifs belong to, or derive from, folktales. For example, there is nothing fantastic in the story of The Sailor and the Oar, however unlikely the means that the protagonist employs to accomplish his quest may be (a man seeking a community unfamiliar with the sea would probably make verbal inquiries rather than walk inland with an oar), and the erotic duel­ ing of Bellerophon and Anteia is neither fantastic nor unrealistic. In order to draw upon fabulous stories, Homer (by whom I mean the poet and/or his tradition) transforms some fabulous motifs into something non-fabulous, as when the magic brand of the Meleager story and the magic ring of the Polyphemos story are changed, as it seems, into curses. More often Homer retains the fabulous while distancing it in some way from the main story. Thus the fabulous adventures recounted in Books 9-12 take place in very distant lands that are set off from the familiar Achaean world, and their narration is assigned to a character within the poem, thereby transferring some responsibility for them to the internal narrator. Although Homer’s epics teem with fabulous elements, they arc not distributed randomly throughout the poems. The regulated presence of the fabulous adds charm and wonder, while the dignity and seriousness of the central story is maintained by the poet’s emphasis on realism and natural causation. There are apparent exceptions to these practices, such as the magical ship of the Phaiakians. In the folktale magical conveyance is employed in order to bring the hero home in an impossibly short period of 462 WILLIAM HANSEN time so that he may arrive before the remarriage of his wife, which he has learned is imminent. But Odysseus faces no such crisis,

for Penelope has scheduled no wedding date, and in any case Odysseus has no precise knowledge of events in Ithaka. In this instance the poet retains the element of the fantastic from the folktale and nar­ rates it in his own voice, but he decouples the role it plays in the folktale from the workings of the epic plot, retaining the wonder of the phenomenon but making nothing crucial depend causally upon the supernatural speed of the Phaiakian vessel. Some non-fabulous motifs have also been modified because in their original form they did not suit the dignity of Greek heroic poetry. It would not be seemly to make Odysseus cut off his finger to rid himself of a magic ring, as the hero of The Ogre Blinded does, nor to have Odysseus prove his identity to his wife by describing her body intimately. The poet’s solution is to transform the magic ring into a curse and to content himself with a less intimate level in the Identity Test. Ralph M. Rosen HOMER AND HESIOD One of the most frustrating aspects of Homeric studies is that so little literary material outside the Homeric corpus itself survives to enhance our understanding of the cultural landscape of the period. Recent scholarship suggests that a large and diverse poetic tradition lay behind the figure we refer to as ‘Homer,’ but little of it survives. Indeed we have little continuous written Greek for another century. The one exception is Hesiod, who composed two extant poems, the Theogony and Works and Days, and possibly several others, including the Shield of Heracles and the Catalogue o f Women. As we shall see, while Hesiodic poetry was not occupied specifically with heroic themes, it was part of the same formal tradition of epic, sharing with Homer key metrical, dialectal, and «fictional features. There are many reasons, beyond chronological proximity, to draw connections between Homer and Hesiod. Both poets composed in the dactylic hexameter, the traditional meter of Greek epic, and in an oral formulaic tradition. Like Homer, Hesiod was primarily con­ cerned with transmitting traditional material in oral performance. Comparative analysis of Homeric and Hesiodic diction indicates that both poets drew on a common store of traditional formulas.' The particular ways in which this heritage manifests itself in both poets suggests that epic was driven by a ‘panhellenic’ impulse, a desire to appeal to as many city-states as

possible. In language and theme alike, therefore, Homeric and Hesiodic poetry represent a movement away from epichoric composition, toward performances that could be intelligible and meaningful virtually anywhere in Greece.* 1 2 These linguistic and formal similarities led ancient critics to see 1 See G. ROSEN Recently, in fact, a number of scholars have been arguing that, well beyond matters of diction, meter, and formula, the Works and Days was perhaps even more profoundly engaged in the Homeric tradition than the Theogony. The Works and Days, after all, is a poem expliddy about cosmic justice (dike) as it manifests itself in the daily lives of human beings. Dike is certainly a multivalent term in Archaic Greek thinking, but as it emerges in the Works and Days, it can be summarized as that sense of

balance and order in human activity most conducive to personal and social well-being in a precarious world. At first glance, this may seem like a theme rather alien to the pre­ dominantly heroic and militaristic world of Homer, where individual Ideas often holds the spotlight and little systematic moralizing can be found on mundane social or domestic issues. But Homeric epic also concerns dike, even if it is there articulated in different ways than it is in the Works and Days. In the broadest sense, the Iliad and Odyssey tell one grand story about how dike operates throughout all stages of human relations, from the interpersonal to the international. The story is told with the kind of authorial distance we come to expect of the epic poet, and there is no pretense, as there is in the Works and Days, of offering practical ‘advice’ to an audience construed in the second person. But while a didactic thread may be less easily traced through Homer than it can in the Works and Days, the funda­ mental ethical issues that inspired the tale of Troy and the nostoi (‘homecomings’) are not far removed from Hesiod’s. In fact, the mythical cause of the Trojan War itself—the abduction of Helen by the foreigner Paris—was a violation of dike at an interpersonal level of the sort that interested Hesiod most. Indeed, throughout the Iliad and the Odyssey the delicate issues of social and material equity, a concern for the proper bfdance of giving and receiving, for time (‘honor’) and philia (‘friendship’), are continually dramatized in some of the most pivotal scenes of both poems: we may recall the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles over Briseis (the event that occa­ sions the very plot of the Iliad), the failed embassy to Achilles’ tent, the behavior of the suitors toward Telemachus at Ithaca, or the complex social dynamics at work in Odysseus’ behavior with the Cyclopes, to name just a few. The dispute between Hesiod and his brother Perses over an inher­ itance of land, which ultimately motivates the composition of the Works and Days (or so Hesiod claims), can be situated in the same general realm of moral discourse as the Homeric examples, even if HOMER AND HESIOD 485 the players are now supposed to be ‘contemporary’ rather than he­ roic.56 5 7 Perses’ violation of dike prompts Hesiod to offer him a pro­ longed sermon

on the dangers of unjust behavior and the need for self-sufficiency through hard work in an agricultural economy. Hesiod’s moralizing, simply put, seeks to promote a world in which humans coexist peacefully, resolve their disputes though law, and regard vio­ lence as itself a violation of dike. Homer’s narrative, by contrast, offers a considerably more complex response to wrongful behavior than Hesiod’s in its focus on heroic figures, who have acquired their exalted status primarily through military expertise and the desire for kleos?1 This is a simplistic evaluation, of course, which hardly does justice to the subtle treatment of the many individual Homeric heroes, but taken together these heroes do represent a contrast to the system of values envisioned by Hesiod. Happy landowners living at peace with each other, constructing their lives in accordance with the rhythms of nature certainly did not form the focus of heroic epic. Introduced by a relative pronoun and some­ times one or more epithets, they may either describe the divinity in the present tense through an account of his typical haunts, pursuits, gifts to mankind, and characteristic activities, or recount a myth about him, often a birth story and an account of his first arrival on Olympus, which may be quite short or go on for hundreds of lines. The mythic and the descriptive modes both serve to reveal the deity’s essential and eternal nature, whether in his characteristic habitual actions or through his unique history. The 45-line Hymn to Pan combines the two modes by first depicting his typical activities, scampering among the mountain nymphs, who then sing a hymn recounting his birth, his introduction to Olympus, and the amused amazement of the gods at his peculiar appearance.22 Hymn 33 to the Dioscuri inverts the pat­ tern by briefly recounting their birth, then their characteristic activ­ ity of rescuing sailors at sea, and ending with a brief narration in the aorist of such a rescue. The verb forms used here and scattered throughout the Hymns resemble the Indo-European injunctive, which characterizes the time­ less activities of the gods.23 To recount a unique event in a god’s history means simultaneously to represent him as he always is. The Hymn to Dionysus (7), whose 59 lines place it between the long and short Hymns, clearly exemplifies this feature of hymnic narrative: the story of the unrecognized god, whom Tyrrhenian sailors abduct and try to bind, and who reveals his divinity, punishing the impious and rewarding those who acknowledge him, constitutes both a singu­ lar event in the god’s story and, at the same time, an eternal manifes­ tation of his divinity. THE HOMERIC HYMNS 499 Others focused on the Hymns as sources for the history of religion or on questions of date and provenance. Recently, however, there has been a revived interest in the Hymns as works of literary art and religious thought. New approaches include studies in the encomiasdc rhetoric of the Hymns, structuralist analyses of the myths embedded in the poems, narratological studies, as well as applications of psycho­ analytic and feminist theory. With their charm, humor, and pathos, the Hymns have finally begun to be restored to their proper τιμή in the history of Greek literature and thought.42 The four major Homeric Hymns all possess an extensive narrative middle section; with the epic they share not only formulaic diction but also narrative techniques such as dialogue and type scenes as well as plot types also found in many kinds of traditional story­ telling.43 But certain recurrent features seem to characterize the long Hymns as a genre. The celebration of the chosen divinity takes the form of a dramatic mythological narrative in which the god is the protagonist and which defines the divinity’s essential function and character through his words and deeds. Despite their differences in style and subject matter, the long Hymns are also linked by a com­ mon mythological framework that gives these compositions a generic unity. Each Hymn recounts a critical moment in the mythological history of the Olympians; the actions and

events that occurred then among the gods have permanent consequences for gods and men and inaugurate a new era in both the divine and human cosmos. Temporally, the framework can be more narrowly defined: the he­ roic epic reveals the fully perfected and stable Olympian pantheon in its interaction with the heroes; cosmogonic poetry, like Hesiod’s Theogony recounts the origins of the primal gods, the emergence of the Olympians, and culminates in the accession of Zeus to the king- ship of the gods. Generically, then, the narratives of Hymns fill the gap between theogonic poetry and heroic epic. Like the panhellcnic epic and the great panhellenic shrines of Delphi, Delos, Eleusis and Olympia, the Olympian pantheon whose development the Hymns describes is a panhellenic construct, in which various divinities with their varied origins and local cults are organized into an ordered 42 Cf. Consequently, the narratives demonstrate an avoidance of local cults and legends and rcjvorkings of local myths in the interests of a pan­ hellenic Olympian orientation.44 Typical components of hymnic narrative include conflict, aetiology, epiphany, and an Olympian scene.45 The birth narratives of Apollo, Hermes, and, doubtless, the fragmentary Hymn to Dionysus constitute ideal subjects since the birth of a new god inevitably precipitates a crisis within the existing order, which is only resolved when he establishes his sphere of influence and is integrated into the Olym­ pian hierarchy. Demeter and Aphrodite likewise proceed from a chal­ lenge to Zeus’ order on the part of female deities, whose outcome leads to a new ordering of relations, not only among the gods, but also between gods and mortals. As the supreme dispenser of τιμαί among the Olympians, Zeus plays a critical, if sometimes unobtrusive, role in the major Hymns. It is he who sanctions his childrens’ privileges and legitimates them in Apollo and Hermes', he also can modify them by increasing or dimin­ ishing the prerogatives of the gods as he does in Demeter and Aphro­ dite. But Zeus reigns as father not only

of gods, but also of men. While the Hymns offer a divine perspective with the gods as the major players, nevertheless, human beings are inevitably involved in these divine dramas. Their roles, in fact, often provide much of the humor and charm in these poems, whether it be Anchises cowering under the bed-clothes as Aphrodite reveals herself, or the naively ignorant daughters of Celeus who welcome the disguised Demeter, or the terrified Cretans who find their ship guided by a giant dol­ phin. But, on a more serious level, the divine conflicts and their resolutions serve to define the human condition: both Apollo and Hermes entail improvements in the primitive state of mankind by instituting closer communication between gods and men through Apollo’s oracle and Hermes’ mediating and civilizing functions. THE HOMERIC HYMNS 503 Demeter Demeter’s combination of charm and solemnity, its familiar and mov­ ing narrative of mother and daughter, which links the cosmic phe­ nomena of the seasons with the divine drama of loss and renewal, has long made it a favorite among the Hymns.55 Culminating in the foundation of the Mysteries at Eleusis, the poem, with its overt aetiological passages, has had special interest for historians of Greek religion, who have discovered in the narrative a counterpart to the initiatory rituals carried out in the sanctuary. Yet the Hymn clearly does not violate the prohibition, enunciated at its end, against rev­ elation of the secret rites. Its date and occasion remain obscure, although the Hymn’s silence concerning Athens has suggested a date before the Athenian takeover of the Mysteries, and many scholars have assigned its performance to a local Eleusinian festival.56 Recently, however, doubts have been raised concerning the author’s knowl­ edge of Eleusinian geography and ritual, as well as Eleusis’ early independence from Athens.57 At any rate, the Hymn cannot be read as the script for the sacred dromena at Eleusis, nor does it present purely local traditions, or those current in 6th century Athens but possibly far older in origin, but rather a unique synthesis designed to

reinforce its panhellenic message. Of late. palatial societies. It is clearly very difficult to connect the specifics of either world, but is there any point of intersection be­ tween the two? Connecting Homer to the Bronze Age? Clearly, any investigation of the topic ‘Homer and the Bronze Age’ must take into account the issue of the chronological and spatial separation of one from the other. In the light of the above discus­ sion, can we demonstrate a continuous tradition of epic song extend­ ing back in time from Homer to the Greek Late Bronze Age? If we can provide an affirmative answer to this question, then it makes more plausible the transmission of some ‘real’ Bronze Age features preserved in the ‘amber* of a continuous epic tradition, although we must not assume that the content of such poetry will remain con­ stant.24 I deal first with the question of continuity of epic song, since, in my opinion, it embodies elements that are—to some extent— independently verifiable. If we can demonstrate its continuity, then we can speculate on the means by which Bronze Age poetry might have become transformed over the Dark Age into epic poems like the Iliad and the Odyssey. The most convincing evidence of the existence of epic in the Bronze Age is linguistic, because such elements arc subconsciously incorpo­ rated in the very fabric of the poems. Some years ago, Janko (1982) demonstrated that Homer’s epic Kunstsprache (and that of Hesiod and the Homeric Hymns) was entirely consistent with the eighth-century linguistic situation in the Ionic-speaking Greek world and that the language was in dynamic transition even within the relatively short span encompassed by Homer, Hesiod, and the composers of the 34 For a discussion of possible phases in the development of epic from the early Mycenaean period through the Dark Age, see Sherratt (1990). 524 JOHN BENNET hymns. Against this background, certain linguistic features stand out as being of considerable antiquity and, with the hindsight afforded by the decipherment of Linear B, it is possible to demonstrate that some of these features must have their origins in the Bronze Age. Most significant among these are elements independent of Greek phonology, a complex area to explore using the syllabic Linear B evidence and the Homeric text as we

have it in its essentially post- Alexandrian form. The most convincing feature in the area of syntax is the use of tmesis (£he separation of verbs from verb particles or preverbs) in Homer. Horrocks (1980; 1984) has shown that the sepa­ ration of verbs from verb particles or preverbs belonged to an early phase of Greek and was also paralleled in Sanskrit. The probability is that this feature of early Greek syntax was retained in the epic, poetic language because of the flexibility it offered in developing formulae within the constraints of the meter. Using Mycenaean evi­ dence as a comparison, however, Horrocks demonstrated that the prose language preserved in the Linear B tablets (dating from c. 1400- 1200 B.C.) appears to use verbal prefixes much as later Greek did, suggesting that this element of the Homeric language went back to a time before that of Linear B: Since these rules arc inherited, since in all probability they have al­ ready disappeared from the Mycenaean prose language, since there are no plausible alternative lines of descent, and since their preserva­ tion in Epic is clearly and strongly motivated by the need to maintain the array of compositional techniques intact, we must conclude that dactylic poetry did indeed have a role to play in the Bronze Age narrative tradition and that certain aspects at least of that tradition passed in a direct line down to the Dark Age. (Horrocks [1980] 9) If Horrocks is correct, then tmesis must have been retained in a poetic language before the time of the Linear B tablets as we have them, certainly before 1200 B.C., the end of the Late Helladic ΙΠΒ phase from which the archives at Pylos, Mycenae, Thebes and Tiryns date, possibly even by 1400 B.C., the date of the earliest preserved Knossos texts. It is not difficult to imagine why the feature would have been retained in poetic language, but the fact that it is not reflected in the (perhaps equally specialized?) language used by the Linear B scribes may have implications for the separation of these different spheres, literate and non-literate (on which, see below). is reflected in our normalized text. Nevertheless, linguists have shown that certain fea­ tures of Homer’s language retain archaic forms where meter demands them. A simple example of this phenomenon is the frequently at­ tested o-stem genitive in -oto, the only o-stem genitive preserved in Linear B, but not preserved in any later Greek dialect, and in the process of being ousted in Homeric epic by the more recent form -ου, where the meter would accommodate it.“ This particular ex­ ample cannot be used to prove the existence of Mycenaean epic, since -oto may have survived the Bronze Age and been incorporated into epic language within its intervening Dark Age stages. The liter­ acy they reflect was a very specialized literacy, a fact that is further reinforced by its total disappearance in the

Closing the Frone: the Bronze Age and Homer It seems that there are a number of senses in which we can relate Homer’s epic poems to the Greek Bronze Age. In the first case, we can plausibly link the techniques of epic oral composition to the world of the Bronze Age palaces, demonstrating a more-or-less continuous tradition of epic song at least from the early Mycenaean period (c. 1700 B.C.) to Homer’s day. The initial development (or elabora­ tion) of such a tradition seems plausible in the context of the reor­ ganization of Mycenaean society that took place in the Shaft Grave period at Mycenae itself and elsewhere, as Sherratt observed (1990). Given that continuity, we can go some way to explaining how some features of the material world of the Bronze Age were preserved in Homeric poetry, while, in our present knowledge of oral poetics, we can well understand why social features—and many linguistic fea­ tures—were systematically and subconsciously modernized through time.35 Is there any way in which Homer the poet self-consciously com­ posed about the Bronze Age? He was creating an epic world explic- idy situated in the past. From Hesiod’s excursus on the different ages (Works and Daps 156-65), we can see that contemporary Greek poets understood their past in terms of a transitional generation—the race of heroes—between the age of bronze and their

own time, that of iron.36 Although Homer—because of the nature of his poetry—does not make the reference explicit like Hesiod, we can assume that this was the age to which he would have attributed the events of his tales. But by the very construction of the system of ages and by the explicit comparison between then and now, Homer and Hesiod both link their eighth-century present to the time of the traditional Trojan War. For eighth-century Greeks it was an unbridgeable gap: it was impossible to demonstrate genealogical continuity across it (i.e., eighth-century inhabitants could not give themselves genealogies extending back into the Bronze Age) and it was equally impossible to demonstrate continuity of authority across the same time period (i.e., eighth-century rulers did not trace their own lineage back to Bronze Age heroes). It seems most likely to me that this disjunction is responsible for much of the explicit aggran­ dizing of the past in Homer, and that Bronze Age epic would have lacked such self-conscious inferiority about contemporary life.37 Because of this disjunction, Homer deliberately creates an ‘epic distance’ between his audience and the events of the poems. For example, although iron appears (particularly in similes, elements that need to be most accessible to contemporary audiences, or as a prize in the games of Patroclus [//. 23.826-35]), bronze is the major metal for weapons in the poems.38 A converse—and more complex—example is the use of writing. Writing is almost entirely absent from the poems and in this respect, we assume Homer’s picture reflects his own society and indeed his own status as an oral poet. Yet we know that at least a certain element of Mycenaean society was literate—an apparent contrast. It is possible, however, that Homer preserves a memory of Bronze Age literacy in the famous Bellerophon

episode and introduces it as yet another example of ‘epic distance.’ Although this is possible, perhaps a more convincing explanation is that the medium—a diptych tab­ let—is the most significant element in the story, reflecting eastern writing practices contemporary with Homer himself, or belonging to the Bronze Age (as the Uluburun diptych now attests). We might think of metals (along with armor, etc.) and writing as elements that Homer deliberately employed to give historical color to his poetry. Other elements, where we have some Bronze Age evidence seem to follow a regular pattern. In particular, certain mate­ rial culture features and status-terms common in the Mycenaean palatial world are attributed to gods in Homer. One of the most striking features of the question, however, is perhaps why Homeric epic sprung up where it did. Bronze Age bard and that of the Iron Age bard (Fig. 1). In Lorimer’s view, Homeric material culture was as much an amalgam as the Homeric Kunstsprache, bearing no more relationship to any real situation than Homer’s language did to any spoken tongue.4 Lorimer used archaeology to challenge some of Schliemann’s con­ clusions, while retaining his assumption that the goals of archaeology were to elucidate the text and, if possible, to date the real heroic world described there. But the post-war re-evaluation of the Iron Age also had more radical results. In 1953, C. G. Starr began work on his Origins of Greek Civilization, aiming to use Iron Age archaeology not as a footnote to literary scholarship, but as a major source for social history. For Starr, Homer was most important as a central figure of what he called ‘the age of revolution’ (c. 750-650 B.C.), in which Classical Greek civilization took shape.5 In the 1970s, A. M. Snodgrass (1971), V. R. Desborough (1972), and J. N. Coldstream (1977) each published a detailed synthesis of Iron Age archaeology. All three books had a massive impact on scholarship, but Snodgrass’ Dark Age of Greece

seems to have been the most influential, taking up Starr’s historical approach. Snodgrass saw the Iron Age artifacts as revealing a period of poverty, isolation, and simplicity, a true ‘Dark Age.’ He took Lorimer’s conflation model of Homeric society further, bolstering it with a comparative argument that Homeric marriages also conflated incompatible practices from different historical periods (Snodgrass [1974]). A second argu­ ment, still a minority position at the time of writing but steadily gaining supporters, bolds that the 1970s ‘Dark Age’ models exaggerated the scale of disruptions after 1200. Those who hold this view sometimes assert that Homerists should return their focus to the Bronze Age.7 In the remainder of this paper, I present a summary of the archaeo­ logical evidence now available from Iron Age Greece (by which I mean the period roughly 1100-700 B.C.). I have two goals in taking this approach to the issue of ‘Homer and the Iron Age.’ The first is that for most Homerists, the 1970s syntheses are still the obvious place to go for an understanding of the material record. New finds have accumulated at an astonishing rate in the last twenty-five years, and although I can only provide a brief sketch in this short chapter, it may nevertheless provide a

useful introduction to the newer materials. My second aim is to show through a collection of the evidence that the kind of assumptions which have guided ‘Homeric archaeol­ ogy’ for most of its brief history—that the archaeologist’s job is to compare the finds with the texts, either to date the real society which Homer describes, or to chart the evolution of our the poems through time—are inappropriate. As archaeologists since Lorimer have repeatedly insisted, the material world described by Homer cannot be paralleled by the excavated record from any single region of Greece at any single point in time within the Iron Age. Archae­ ologists have generally assumed that this means that a series of Dark Age poets described the lost race of heroes in terms of the material culture of their own times, that oral composition somehow ‘froze’ different bits and pieces of the material world into the poems, and that in Homer we have a mixture of all these chronological layers, which wc can excavate (much like an archaeological site).8 Instead, I make an argument much like Snodgrass’ (this vol.): material culture and poetic culture were two ways in which people in eighth-century Greece constructed the social world within which they moved. Both were important arenas in which people fashioned images of what they wanted their world to be, and challenged competing construc­ tions which they did not like. Reducing either to a passive reflection of the other is simplistic. I conclude that there is no way to use Iron Age archaeology to fix Homer in time or space; rather, Iron Age verbal and non-verbal representations must be read together, as sources for a fuller cultural history. Strong regional variation i$ typical of Iron Age Europe, and Greece is no exception. Consequently, I divide the Greek world into four areas. Central Greece, where Homer’s supposed homes of Smyrna and Chios lie, has attracted most archaeological activity, and I describe it in rather greater detail that the other regions.9 Central Greece Chronology

In Middle Protogeometric and most of Late Protogeometric, almost all these metal goods, whether weapons or ornaments, were iron. Bronze, gold, and silver all but disappear. Snodgrass argues that the shift to iron grave goods around 1025 was the start of a true iron-using economy. He suggests that central Greeks learned iron-working from Cyprus before 1050, but by 1025 long-distance trade had collapsed. Cut off from tin and copper, cen­ tral Greeks began to make all their metal objects out of iron, even delicate ornaments. He saw this as but one facet of a broader trans­ formation: as population continued to lall, large areas of Greece were left empty altogether, and new egalitarian, tribal, and perhaps pasto­ ral/ nomadic social forms emerged. This is a powerful thesis, but there are other facets of the evi­ dence which also need to be brought out. The fall in numbers of graves is pardy caused by a change in their age structure: few child burials dating to the period after 1025 have be found, and fewer still after 900. The only demographically plausible interpretation of these age structures is that most children were disposed of in Protogeometric through Middle Geometric times in ways which have low archaeo­ logical visibility. I have argued that the visibility issue goes further, and that a new ritual system emerged around 1025/1000, imposing order on the chaos of Submycenaean times. The new funerary re­ gime drew boundaries within the community: not only between adults and children, but also among the adults, between an elite and a larger, lower group. The elite represented itself as internally egalitar­ ian, while the lower classes—like the children—received relatively informal disposal. Gender distinctions within the elite were only lightly marked. There is good evidence for Snodgrass’ model of a collapse of trade at the end of the eleventh century, since Greek objects disappear from Near Eastern contexts in this period, and Philistine pressure on the Phoenician cities provides a plausible context. But we must also understand the exclusive use of iron grave goods in ritual context: regardless of economic realities—or perhaps because of them—iron was a potent symbol. It drew lines between the present and the bronze­ using past, and between the local soil, the source of iron ore in most parts of

Greece, and the broader eastern world from which exotic items and the raw materials for making bronze came. As Hesiod was later to say, this was truly a race of iron. Next to him was a female inhumation, decked out in gold jewelry. One piece was already a thousand years old when buried, and came from Baby­ lon. An adjacent shaft held four horses. Over the graves was a giant krater and a fifty-meter long apsidal building. The building was deliberately filled in and converted into a tumulus. The most important thing about these finds is not that they are just richer than contemporary burials: rather, their symbol­ ism turns on its head everything that we see in the rest of central Greece. Where other burials are inward-turned and homogeneous, cutting the present ofT from the past, and the Aegean off from the Near East, these graves do just the opposite. It was perhaps in the turbulent years around 1000 B.C., when every aspect of ritual was changing, that the Greek concept of the hero crystallized, as the mirror image of the present as a sadly declined race of iron. A vast amount of wealth was drained into religious architecture. Some sites had spectacular votives, including thousands of bronzes and impres­ sive Near Eastern and Egyptian objects. Weapons, rich jewelry, and Near Eastern imports disappeared from central Greek graves at just the time that they became common in sanctuaries, and Snodgrass ([1980] 54) has argued that ‘There is a big social change with the redirection of attention towards the communal sanctuary and away from the individual grave.’ Some eighth-century sanctuaries may have been sacred across the whole Iron Age. At Ephesus and Iria on Naxos there are hints of continuous activity, but in most cases where temples stood above Bronze Age shrines material evidence breaks off by 1100, and there is a stratigraphic gap until 900 or later. Ayia Irini on Kea is an intriguing case. Here, the head of a Mycenaean figurine was used as a cult image in the sixth century, while the body lay sealed in a twelfth-century layer. There are many possible explanations for these finds, but the most economical is that cult continued across the elev­ enth and tenth centuries, but in forms which left few material traces, only to change drastically around 750. HOMER AND THE IRON AGE 547 The space of the living was transformed just as much as the spaces of the dead and the gods. At Megara Hyblaea, a colony founded in Sicily in 728, the settlers left an open space in the center of the town for an agora. For the first time, circuit walls become common around 700, protecting settlements against attack but also marking them off from the countryside. The most profound changes came within settle­ ments. Multi-room, rectilinear houses focused on internal courtyards replaced the old Dark Age curvilinear single-room houses. At Zagora, the process was almost complete before 700, and in the Euboean colony of Pithekoussai an oval hut was rebuilt as a rectilinear house around 725. At Miletus, oval huts continued alongside more com­ plex structures in the seventh century, but here too one hut was rebuilt as a rectangular house before 650, and by 600 the shift to courtyard houses was complete. The courtyard house was an important innovation. To live among such closed-in houses, which could only be entered through a nar­ row

door onto the street, was a different experience from the open space of a Dark Age village. This may have been most important in gender ideologies: in later literature the enclosed, dark, inner rooms of a house were associated with the female and opposed to the open, light, public spaces of male citizens. Yet another spatial transformation was the collapse of distance. Thucydides (1.13) claimed that the trireme was invented around 700,16 and we see a huge increase in finds of Greek pottery in other parts of the Mediterranean. Thucydides (6.3-5) also dates the first colony in Sicily to 733, and cross-dating with Egypt roughly confirms this. Thousands of Greeks emigrated between 750 and 700, which sup­ ports the picture of rapid population growth. Colonization probably played a key part in the feverish social experiments of these years. A reordering of time paralleled this reordering of space. Another Near Eastern import, writing, provided new ways to fix information across time, and was crucial to the formation of the epics themselves (Powell, this voL). Some Semitidsts argue that ‘the alphabet’ was invented as early as the eleventh century; there is no direct evidence for this, but even if such claims prove to be correct, there was never­ theless a drastic change in the use of writing in Greece after 750. But nonetheless, Iron Age society was permanendy transformed. The world of the city-states had been created, a world of farmer-citizens unlike any­ thing we find in the rest of the Iron Age Mediterranean. For him, as well as dealing with chronological layering, ‘the problem [is] of sifting out those aspects which may refer to one type of society, and those which refer to another/ These are important observations, but both approaches seem to me to lose sight of the fact that the epics and the material record were both produced by real people, acting in pursuit of their own goals in a period of dramatic change. They represent the relation­ ships between verbal and non-verbal culture as being mechanical: for Coldstream and Whitley, and for many other

archaeologists (and historians), Homer is a mirror to an external materiality, but a defective one. Our job is then to smooth out his distorting surface to produce a clear reflection of the realities of Homer’s world. Against these views, I would insist that the epic was not some kind of bad history. It was a poetic creation, what some eighth-century Greeks thought the heroic world ought to have been like. I suggested above that in the rituals which produced the archaeological record, Iron Age Greeks manipulated material culture as a non-verbal language through which they debated who they were and where they stood relative to each other, the larger east Mediterranean world, and the lost heroic past. The ritualized performance of epic poetry, although its only material trace is a body of texts refracted through centuries of reworking and copying,26 was also a key part in this process. The poets described the heroes as using specific kinds of objects in order to create desired states of mind among their hearers. Nagy ([1990a] 10) suggests that Homer ‘synthesizes the diverse traditions of each major city-state into a unified pan-Hellenic model that suits the ideology of the polls in general, but without being restricted to the ideology of any one polis in particular.’ Similarly, Homer uses objects—some contemporary, some ancient, some in­ vented—to evoke the past in the present, creating an ‘epic distance.’ Objects were as manipulable as language, religion, and the laws of physics, and there is no point in trying to pull Homer’s picture apart, reassembling it in ‘layers’ which can then be correlated with the artifacts found in discrete archaeological strata. We should rather think of the epics themselves as artifacts—arguably the most impor­ tant, for modem classicists as for ancient Greeks—generated in the great upheavals of the eighth century. The poems and the archaeo­ logical record can only be properly understood when read alongside each other and woven together, as remnants of competing eighth- century efforts at self-fashioning, out of which classical Greek civili­ zation was created. A nthony Snodgrass HOMER AND GREEK ART Ever since an approximate historical setting

was established for the final form of the Homeric poems, it has been natural to look for comparisons with other phenomena of the same era, and especially with the visual arts. Today there is a long-standing consensus that, in art-historical terms, that setting is to be placed within the epoch of the Geometric style, and more specifically toward its latter end. Geometric art has therefore been the favored field for this kind of comparative study; but that is not the whole story. For such study may have many different goals: to measure the impact of the poems on Greek society, either initially or in the longer term; to add pre­ cision to the dating of the poems; to interpret the works of art in the light of the poems; to discern common structures in the literary and artistic creations. Some of these approaches involve extending the investigation to later periods of art as well. Nearly all of them share another assumption, that first place must be given to the better understanding of the poems. Such a priority will come naturally to anyone who knows Homer but, again, it should not be the whole story. It may not be coincidental that one of the most fruitful fields of investigation has been one which to some extent adopts the oppo­ site priority: the study of those passages in Homer that describe or refer to works of art, in the light of the surviving art of the period. It is, for example, a neat and objective confirmation of the relative dating of the Iliad and the Aspis that the artistic description of the Shield of Achilles in the former suggests an object stylistically earlier than the Shield of Herakles in the latter.1 In this chapter, however, I must be selective. I will concentrate on the art of the period which has the best claim to have fallen within the actual lifetime of Homer, the Late Geometric: a conservative choice, but one modified by the adoption of a less traditional aim, that of keeping the literary and the visual elements in more or less equal balance. For the truth is that the well-tried approaches have 1 For this genera! topic, see Fittschen (1973); Canciani (1984). HOMER AND GREEK ART 561 been less fruitful than their early exponents must have hoped. They have suffered by sharing a form of positivism that is very familiar in

archaeology: the belief that what survives today, because it is all that we have as a basis for inference, must be assumed to have held a place of equal prominence in its own world. In this case there is, on the literary side, every encouragement for that belief: the Homeric poems are part of what survives, and the testimony to their excep­ tionally influential and prominent position in Greek life, extending far beyond the purely literary sphere, is almost limidess. Yet even here, prominence is not the same thing as near-isolation, which is their position today. Other equally early epic poetry with legendary content (even the surviving work of Hesiod; see Rosen, this vol.) and, above all, other orally-transmitted mythology in non-literary forms, are often forgotten in the urge to match the two surviving epics with the visual material—with the former almost always filling the role of the model, the latter that of the naive imitator. The artistic material too, with much less justification, is regularly assumed to be at least a representative sample and sometimes more, the very cream, of what the Greeks of the age could produce. Thus the stage has been set for the long and, in my view, unsuccessful history of the attempts to identify legendary episodes—if posable, specifically Homeric episodes— in the figure-scenes shown in Geometric art. But the underlying assumptions could hardly have survived a pro­ longed and cool reflection on the facts of the case. We know of too many legends that are not contained in the Iliad, and the Odyssey, and we can prove that contemporary artists knew of them too. We can infer, not least from a reading of Homer himself, the existence of other media for artistic representation for which the physical evi­ dence no longer survives. With such material as does survive, we have few reasons for thinking that it occupied a central place in the cultural life of Greece as a whole. Finally, there are chronological questions still open to discussion today: we cannot be so precise in the relative dating of the literary and the artistic evidence that we can always deduce the direction in which a perceived influence was travelling. Once we acknowledge the fragmentary and, in the case of the artistic material, fortuitous nature of our evidence, it becomes clear that fresh approaches are needed. Instead of ‘matching9 one class of material with another, we

shall do better to concentrate on integrat­ ing all of it into a very incomplete picture of the intellectual life of 562 ANTHONY SNODGRASS the period. At the most, we may discover what could arouse the enthusiasm of a few scattered and probably socially exclusive groups in different parts of the Greek world, a world that had already grown to the point where two of its communities could be living a thou­ sand miles apart. We may turn to the comparison of ‘Homer’ and contemporary ‘Greek art,’ in the realization that it is going to be difficult to keep the comparison a balanced one. Where Homer was treasured by later Greeks, Geometric art was not; where Homer grew to be a panhellenic figure, the art of Geometric Greece was divided into a number of regional styles which had a limited appeal beyond their own orbit. A further problem arises, in that there is at first sight so great a discrepancy in sophistication between the poetry of Homer and the work of his contemporaries the graphic artists, working mainly but not entirely in the medium of painting in silhouette on vases of the Late Geometric style, that it seems a presumption to compare or link them. To take first just the issue of characterisation: on the one hand, we have a mastery of presentation that uses words and actions to give individuality to even quite minor characters, and at times gives them even their own pattern of speech. On the other, we have the apparently jejune convention of two-dimensional, dark-on-light depiction which seems to allow only of grouping humankind into basic categories: there are men, women and children; within the category of men, warriors and non-warriors; within the category of warriors, winning and losing warriors; but that appears to be as far as characterisation can go. It is hard for these two art-forms reach out and touch each other. The conventional response has been to try to extract specific correspondences of episodes between the poems and the paintings but, as already indicated, that path will not be followed here. The contrast that I have just drawn is not entirely imaginary; but it is, from one point of view, an unfair one. No one now doubts that Homer was the heir to a very long tradition of poetic composition in the same medium that he used himself. Homer’s genius was his own,

but what really set him apart from the visual artists was the wealth of pre-existing material which he could re-shape and elaborate in his own style. There were his predecessors, treating of the same or allied topics, and there were the formulae of poetic phrasing which he either took over from them or else invented himself and then used repeat­ edly. By contrast, the visual artists were only in his lifetime re-inventing HOMER AND GREEK ART 563 a means of representing the human figure in scenes of action. Their art was at a stage of development that epic poetry had passed through generations earlier. But on top of all the inherited skills that Homer could use, there was a new element: the written word (see Powell, this vol.). The interaction between alphabetic writing and the Homeric epic is admittedly controversial, but we at least know that the recording of hexameter lines was one of the earliest uses to which the new script was put in the Greek world; and that sooner rather than later it was used to record Homer’s masterpieces for posterity. By con­ trast, once again, the uses of the written word in the visual arts were apparently not yet conceived of. Long before the notion arose of giving a title to the complete work of art, the simpler expedient of labelling one or more figures in a composition with their names was adopted, thus adding a second means, together with the action por­ trayed, to help the spectator read the narrative. But Homer’s con­ temporaries made do without even this modest aid. For about a hundred years, at a time when the,use of painted or incised ’cap­ tion’ inscriptions was both technically and intellectually a possibility, it was avoided: when painted inscriptions do first appear on vases, they are not of this kind. We tend to explain this avoidance, as we do most things in the art of this period, as the result of pure lack of development; to imagine the possibility that it might have been deliberate is to take a first, speculative step toward re-assessing the purposes behind these early compositions. The introduction of this word, ‘composition,’ is likewise an open­ ing for one kind of comparison between literature and art. In the visual arts, the word has a rather specialized and specific use. It is a very rough synonym for ‘arrangement;’ it covers the

way in which a painter or sculptor arranges the components of his work. It may include the way in which individual figures are posed, especially if they are on a large scale in relation to the work as a whole; but not, for example, their physiognomy or their coloring. As such, it covers decidedly only a part of the artist’s whole range of activity. In litera­ ture or in music, by contrast, ‘composition’ is so absolutely central to the artist’s activity that it is often used as a term for his whole art. Nevertheless, in the case of Homer we have special circumstances, as we have already seen. For Homer was presenting characters many of whom would be already familiar to his audience, through either the medium of earlier poetry or that of vernacular legend; the out- 564 ANTHONY SNODGRASS line of his plots, too, would be a given element shared with his lis­ teners. What ‘composition’ meant for him, what raised him above all his predecessors and his successors alike, was a matchless skill in filling out these characters and plots through his gift for language, and in adding whole new elements to both. Some characters, mostly minor but conceivably including such a memorable figure as Patroclus in the Iliad, we suspect him of having invented himself. There were limits to what the visual artists could do to match this: we have seen some of the inhibitions under which they labored. The vase-painters chose to follow an austere set of conventions, which we believe were first devised by a single personality, known to spe­ cialists as the Ttipylon Master’ and working in Athens in the years around 750 B.C. Neither, at first, did artists in other media make any radical departure from these conventions, for at this time the art of vase-painting in Greece appears to have enjoyed more influence than ever again. Not only was the general principle of silhouette representation taken over from the painted figures on the Geometric vases and, as far as was appropriate, applied to other arts—in three- dimensional compositions, for instance, arrangement into a single plane was adopted, so that a clear profile view predominated; but the actual style of the vase-painter’s silhouettes was also widely imi­ tated, with such features as the human torso in the form of an in­ verted isosceles triangle, or the flaring muzzle of the horse, appearing across

a range of different media.2 These conventions were, as has been said, austere ones: they pre­ scribed a fairly narrow range of attitudes for the human figure, in which the delineation of the body itself was modified as little as possible. This meant that there was no easy way for one figure to be made distinguishable from others. Yet it would be wrong to con­ clude that all potential for narrative was thereby excluded. It was still possible to depict distinctive situations, especially those involving a number of figures, in which the relation between the figures gave the whole work a fairly dear narrative content. It was even possible, in prindple at least, to make that content unique, not just in a trivial sense of combining details in a way not'exactly matched before, but in that of conveying a unique meaning to the onlooker. Even in such a case, ‘composition’ would still not be achieving quite the aim that it did in Homer’s hands, but there are parallels. The term 2 This important argument was first advanced by Robertson (1951). HOMER AND GREEK ART 565 ‘formula’ has often been used of Geometric painting as well (cf. Schein, this vol.), to denote the recurrent elements or ‘building blocks’ with which the artists, like Homer, worked. Just as Homer could compose memorable passages using almost entirely formulaic phrases, so as we shall see the painters could combine their convention-bound fig­ ures into memorable scenes. There is also a different point that could be made about the sub­ jects of the paintings. It has been universally assumed that these are works with a conscious message that the viewer was expected to pick up: that is, works with a ‘subject’ or implicit ‘title.’ But suppose that we return to our point about composition, and make a quite differ­ ent assumption, that ‘subject’ or ‘title’ were secondary adjuncts for the artists, and that their prime concern was with composition for its own sake. We could then invoke the parallel of many painters of later millennia, who allocated titles and subjects, almost casually, to compositions which they had already executed. One such painter who is notorious, justifiably or otherwise, for having given subjects to his paintings without apparently modifying them in more than mar­ ginal ways, is Claude Gellee, or ‘le Lorrain’ (1600-1682). An exhibi­ tion of his works was mounted in the National Gallery in

London in 1994, with the aim of counteracting the view that I have just re­ ferred to, by emphasizing ‘how important the subjects of his pictures were to the artist and his patrons, and how far they determined the form of his compositions.’ But I would still venture the opinion that on many occasions Claude did not let the entitlement of his pictures, with or without the addition of appropriate human figures, distract him from his main aim, of composing one hauntingly beautiful land­ scape after another. If the Geometric vase-painters, like Claude and others, were less interested in the subjects of their pictures than in the way that their scenes were composed; if their dominant aim was the effect of the composition as a composition, then not only would this then ally them more closely with Homer and the literary act of composition, but it would profoundly affect the way in we would look at their products. Instead of feeling frustration at our failure to pick up the intended message—and, a fortiori, to match it with a story in Homeric or other mythology—we could view and at times admire their figure- scenes as pure exercises in composition. The virtual absence of land­ scape and background detail, the restricted use of the dimension of depth, and the complete reliance on a simple dark-on-light contrast. 566 ANTHONY SNODGRASS are of course severe constraints on the effect that they could achieve with their medium; in this sense, the proper comparison is with line­ drawing rather than with landscape painting. Our prime concern is with the figure-scenes, but it must always be remembered that these comprise only a fraction of the painters’ output: the greater part of their time was spent in applying the apparendy abstract geometric decoration which has given its name to the style of the time, and which covers many complete vases, as well as the subsidiary zones of those which carry figure-scenes. If, as has sometimes been argued, elements of this ‘abstract decoration’ in fact carried objective conno­ tations, then it is all the more essential to associate the human figures, equally ‘geometric’ in their own way, with the overall design of the vessel, when we attempt to assess the aims of the artists. It is time to turn to some examples of their work, which I will present in what is believed to be their approximate chronological order.

The Dipylon Master himself painted a funerary scene on a huge mixing-bowl or krater, which stood as a marker over an Athe­ nian grave of about 750 B.C. (Plate 1). There is some independent evidence that bowls of this type were reserved for male graves, and so it is appropriate that here we are shown the lying in state of a deceased male, and that the scenes are of an inherendy male content. The dead man lies on the bier, surrounded by adult and juvenile male mourners. The otherwise common rule of a single base-line for the human figures is violated here. Above, on a higher plane, seated female mourners share the same gesture of the hands raised to the head, perhaps tearing at their hair. Other mourners are grouped in ‘boxes’ at the upper left and upper right. Two prominent chariots drive by, each with a driver and a warrior with a distinctive type of shield that we shall see again repeatedly; a further wheeled vehicle was also probably present in the upper left box, and there are more in the next zone below. A warship is visible under the handle to the right Much of the representational repertoire of the Geometric painter is already deployed here: man, woman, child, the living and the dead, bier, horse, chariot, ship and an unmistakeable form of shield. What we are seeing is perhaps less how a prominent Athenian was buried, than how he would wish to have been buried: it is an impressive scene, with well over forty participants, and details such as the chari­ ots and the warship are often supposed to be allusions to the man’s experience in life. But then we look round the main zone, out of the picture to the left, and we find that there is a rival focus of activity HOMER AND GREEK ART 567 to the standard funerary ritual; for a duel or confrontation is appar­ ently taking place in which a striding figure on the left (we have only the legs) faces a pair of warriors standing very close together in iden­ tical pose. To understand this part of the composition, we shall have to look at some better-preserved examples of the theme: for the moment, we must content ourselves with the fact that it is a recur­ rent theme; that it does offer the artist an unexpected opening for something which

I have said was otherwise difficult for him, the creation of a figure or figures that were distinguishable from others; and that the inclusion of this theme may prove hard to reconcile with the orthodox interpretation of this scene as an episode of real life, or rather real death, in contemporary Athens. Next, an artist from the same circle painted an action scene on a krater of the same purpose (Plate 2), perhaps a little later than the first. Here the picture is preserved in even more fragmentary form, but the action nonetheless appears less intractable to interpretation. In the upper zone, a grim land-battle is taking place: three warriors with rectangular shields are at grips with their enemies, with varying fortunes: one delivers a coup de grace, a second has been shot through the head by an archer, a third is again delivering a death-blow to an opponent with the distinctive shield that we saw in the previous scene, as he fafls from a raised platform that is probably a wheeled vehicle, on which are visible the limbs of dead or wounded companions, lying like their stricken counterparts to the left. Below, three more bearers of this type of shield hurry along, with raised left feet, no doubt to join the fray before it is too late. But then, to the left of them, we are brought up short by another apparition: a shieldless warrior again confronts a pair standing close together: this time, a little more of the combatants is visible and the pair look as if their bodies are actually joined together. The theme has made its second appear­ ance, and I would cut short further speculation by showing a third instance (there are fourteen in all in early Greek art), this time painted on a vessel from Argos, not from Athens (Plate 3). Here I think it is hard to doubt any longer that what we are looking at is a pair of Siamese Twins, a conclusion that will seem less outlandish when we take other evidence into account later. But we must also acknowl­ edge the orthodox, or at any rate the skeptical, interpretation, which is that this motif has changed its meaning with the passage of time: the Argive piece is somewhat later, perhaps around 720-710 B.G., and this view would have it that the image had previously been 568 ANTHONY SNODGRASS intended to

convey nothing more remarkable than two warriors stand­ ing side by side, just as we saw horses side by side and overlapping in the first picture, until someone thought to give it a new twist by converting or distorting it into a portrayal of Siamese Twins. I com­ ment no further at this stage. Our next vase is of a different type, a wine- or water-jug now in the Louvre, whose state of preservation is such that it must have been buried actually within an Athenian grave of perhaps 730 B.C (Plate 4). It has been known for a long time, but it had to wait until 1961 before the scene on it was given a really convincing interpre­ tation.3 Fifteen human figures and one still unexplained apparition are shown. Four of them—numbers 3, 6, 11 and 13 in the projected drawing—adopt gestures that we have not previously seen in quite this form: 6 and 11 grab at the helmet-crests of their opponents with, once again, the distinctive form of shield (5 and 10); while 3 and 13 are lunging for the side-arms carried by their similarly-equipped opponents, 2 and 12. This is surely a scene of the disarming of defeated prisoners. But something more sinister is going on as well: no. 9 has drawn his sword, evidently to use it on no. 8, whom he is gripping by the arm (this detail is obscured by the division of the projected drawing at this point), while further round no. 1 is also on the point of drawing his sword—note the violently flexed elbow. With the enemy already in a state of submission, this is unexpected. But an explanation is given by the collapsing no. 4, and the apparently already dead nos. 7 and 14. The enemy are being disarmed and then butchered: the three figures already stricken are presumably meant to have been laid low by the outstretched weapons which their left-hand neighbours, 3, 6 and 13, still hold above their bodies. The conventions of the human figures are fundamentally unchanged: most of them stand on a common base-line, and they all share the Geometric convention of profile heads and legs, combined with fron­ tal torsos. Four—all on the losing side—carry a type of shield that we have seen repeatedly, together with the regular sword and dagger at the waist. But within the Geometric conventions, one artist at least shows

us what composition can do: consider the effect that he achieves by gesture, from the vain pleading of no. 8 to the grim determination of no. 9, and the way that no. 13 rocks back on his heels, reveling in the violence. See Himmelmann-Wildschütz (1961). HOMER AND GREEK ART 569 Next we turn to another jug, of similar date, and again Athenian (Hate 5). Its main scene is this time not on the body but on the neck: a warship of the type we have seen before is shown capsized; eleven members of the crew are around it, every one clinging on either to the ship, or to a companion who in turn grasps the ship, with fishes in among them. Their torsos are cross-hatched, an early sign of the growing urge to variegate the blank silhouette of Geo­ metric art with internal lines. The latest interpretation of this scene4 suggests that one crewman is destined to perish, the man who lies along the keel to the right, in a pose which we have seen before, sinking downwards with strongly-flexed right arm: this, it is proposed, was a ‘formula’ for a dying figure. All the others, especially of course the man who is astride the keel and is even now giving aid to two companions, have on this view a chance of surviving. It is a grim scene, but less so than the previous one. Our next example takes us away from painted pottery and away from Athens. On the neck of a transport jar, made perhaps around 700 B.C. in Homer’s native region of Ionia, but actually found far to the west in the early Greek settlement of Pithekoussai on the is­ land of Ischia, appears the impression from a stone stamp, showing an armed warrior rescuing the body of an unarmed but gigantic companion: the living warrior simultaneously brandishes two spears (Plate 6). Remarkably, a series of impressions from the very same stone was found on a terracotta plaque, this time not only made but also found in Ionia, in the sanctuary of Hera on the island of Samos. The technique of the carving is, given the difference of material, essentially the same as that in the paintings: solid figures outlined and set off against a blank background. Here, for the first time, we can go a step further in interpretation than in the earlier cases: the iconography

of the scene is one that we believe we can recognise from later pictures, in which the addition of inscribed names makes identification possible. Given that the later convention for the walk­ ing or running attitude of the living figure had not yet been devised, this iconography is more or less exactly that used for the scene of Ajax heroically carrying the dead Achilles from the battlefield at Troy (Hate 7): note how the gigantic size of Achilles is emphasized throughout This interpretation of the scenes on the early stone stamps is not quite an inescapable one: it is still possible, following a 4 See Ahlberg-Comell (1992) 27-28. 570 ANTHONY SNODGRASS line of argument of which we have already heard an example, to suggest that a theme of no very distinctive import was picked up by later artists to convey a story by then well-known—an episode in fact from the Aet/iiopis, one of the ‘Epic Cycle’ of poems, whose action was set before, between or after the two Homeric poems and which were not held to be by Homer. We have only fragments and digests of them, but from these it is usually judged that they were composed some time after Homer. Again, I offer no comment of my own as yet. Our final scene is equally late, around or even just after 700 B.C. A conical stand for a bowl, painted and probably found in Athens, is decorated with eleven human figures and a bird, all large in scale (Plate 8a). What was probably meant to be the central group por­ trays two men with what looks like a scepter between them, in the act Of exchanging swords: behind each of them stands a woman, both carrying branches and the one on the right also holding a baldric which is evidently to form part of the exchange; a fifth figure, a man, comes up from the left carrying game on a stick over his shoul­ der. As we move round the stand to the right, we come first to the bird, next to two warriors who are engaged in combat over the fallen body of a third warrior: over him, a sword and baldric apparently hover in the air (Plate 8b). On the analogy of later convention, we should take this to represent the spoils for which the two men are fighting. Then if we move in the opposite

direction from the central group, we again come upon a duel: and it is perhaps no longer a surprise that one side consists of a pair of twin figures, this time fairly clearly with their bodies joined together. A vertical spiral di­ vides them from the other duelling group. By now, the Geometric conventions have become considerably diluted: most of the figures have visible eyes, and are no longer entirely or even mainly in sil­ houette technique. Yet the spirit of the representation is unchanged: the figures still obey the rule of frontal torsos and profile heads and legs; muscles may be more naturalistically indicated, but the shape of the torso, for example, still follows that of the Geometric isosceles triangle. This, and the fact that the stand may have been painted just within Homer’s lifetime, will I hope excuse its inclusion here. We have seen only a sample of the Geometric figure-painter’s range: but I think it is enough to show how he adapted his composition to the different demands of burial, death in battle, after battle and at sea, rescue and truce. Every one of these themes occurs prominently HOMER AND GREEK ART 571 in the Homeric epics; but what we have not been able to achieve is a specific reading of the narratives that is in any way comparable with our reading of Homer’s. That is not to say that such a read­ ing would have been impossible for his contemporaries too, though the conventions of Geometric art may make it hard to avoid that conclusion. The traditional solution of the impasse, that the pictures were actually meant to illustrate the epic stories, has been referred to earlier on. It is a fact that every one of the scenes we have looked at has, by different scholars at different times and on the basis of different arguments, been claimed to do just that To evaluate such claims, we shall need to look briefly at the sequence once again: but first let us consider what effect the claims, if validated, would have. In many opinions, including apparently those of most Classicists, they would greatly enhance the interest of the paintings: they would offer vital evidence on a question where we badly need it, namely that of the date at which familiarity with the stories told in the epics became widespread enough to feature in the art of Athens,

Argos and other regions besides the poet’s native Ionia. Thus a terminus would at least be fixed for the final stage of the composition of the poems. One is again reminded of the claim for the ‘importance’ of Claude’s subjects for himself and his patrons. But there is a price for acceptance of these claims as well. They would depreciate the achievement of the painters, not only in the obvious sense of making mere illustrators out of them, but more specifically in making them such ineffective illustrators. As we shall see again in a moment, if the prime purpose was really to recall to the viewer’s mind the episodes that he or she had heard recited in the Homeric epics, then the artists cannot be said to have made a success of it: on the contrary, they alternately threw away opportu­ nities and set up obstacles to understanding. I should say now that in my own view, none of the works that we have seen is susceptible to such a reading: only by flady disregarding a whole series of more or less subde signals from the artists can we maintain it. One or two of the identifications have I think been conclusively discredited. But let us test out such claims on the specific instances that we have been looking at. With the first two paintings on funerary kraters (Plates 1-2), the issue is the same. The potential significance of the twin-figures who make such apparendy casual appearances in them hinges upon a 572 ANTHONY SNODGRASS remarkable feature of Greek legend, that it does contain a pair of Siamese Twins. Their deformity is explicitly described by Hesiod (fr. 17B M-W) in a fragment of a poem of much the same date as the latest of the Geometric pictures that we saw. Homer does not dwell on their physical abnormalities, but he does twice involve them briefly in narratives (Iliad 11.709-710, 750-52; 23.638-40): in both cases, they feature in the accounts given by Nestor, at Troy, of the doings of his distant youth. They encounter Nestor in combat where, according to him, they are lucky to escape with their lives; and they also get the better of him in a chariot-race at some funerary games. It is the first occasion which is of potentially more direct relevance here, even though we note that the pictures offer a loose context both of chariotry

and more generally of burial ritual and perhaps funeral games. But did these two artists really mean to recall the episode in Book 11 of the Iliad where Nestor relates his encounter with the Twins? Officially (though not in reality) the sons of Aktor, they were ‘ just lads, unversed in serious fighting’, he says at their first mention; and presently we hear that Ί would have killed the sons of Aktor too... had not their father Poseidon whisked them out of the battle, shrouding them in mist.’ Can these scenes have been intended to illustrate that passage? If so, the artists behaved almost as if they were covering their tracks, surrounding the incident of the Twins with much inappropriate and un-Homeric detail. It is important to note that Nestor’s two reminiscences are not the only stories that we hear about the Siamese Twins: we know that they were eventually waylaid and killed by Herakles in an episode that goes unmentioned in Homer. That the twins are the same pair that is known from legend is overwhelmingly likely; but to insist that the episode chosen must be the same one that Homer chose seems to me to be an example (to use no harsher term) of wishful thinking. With our next picture (Plate 4), it was once argued that two of the figures, nos. 5 and 8, were Ajax and Hector exchanging gifts, when their inconclusive combat was interrupted by a truce (Iliad 7.274— 312); and that 6 and 13 were the two heralds Idaios and Talthybios who separated them. But we saw enough of this picture to realise that such an interpretation simply disregards a number of clear sig­ nals from the artist, above all the wealth of gesture: nor has the surrounding action anything in common with the staged single com­ bat of the Iliad. The shipwreck scene (Plate 5) was a predictable candidate for HOMER AND GREEK ART 573 assimilation with the shipwreck of Odysseus as described in Odyssey 12.403-425; and this time the identification found much more wide­ spread support. But it falls foul of the same criticism as in the previous case: that the artist has used subdety of composition to indicate a very different potential outcome from that of the disaster where Odysseus alone, straddling the keel, survived. If his intention had been to portray the episode from Homer, then he could have done

so very much more simply, by omitting the tell-tale feature of the hands gripping the ship and the limbs of comrades. With the stone stamp-impressions (Plate 6), we are dealing with a different category of inference: here, for the first time, we can enlist a known later iconography in support of an identification of Ajax with the dead Achilles. As we saw, this need not be entirely conclu­ sive: but, when all the evidence is taken into account, it does seem to me more likely than not that this is indeed the intended subject. But here we encounter a new factor of a quite different kind: of all the epic identifications we have considered, this is the only one where the episode in question is not from Homeric epic. The rescue of Achilles’ body is not an event related by Homer; it belongs instead to the Aelhiopis, an epic which Greek tradition and the surviving frag­ ments alike suggest was composed, in its final form, well after either Homer or the date of the stamps. This is a salutary finding for two reasons: first, it reminds us that Homer was not the exclusive source for legends of the Heroic Age; and especially not for the artists since, over the whole of the first century or so of Greek figure-scenes, incor­ porating this period and the ensuing one, only a small fraction of the probable mythological scenes take their subject from the Iliad or the Odyssey—between 10% and 16%, according to the degree of optimism of the person counting.5 Secondly, it hints that neither need epic poetry as a whole have been such an exclusive source. The Homeric interpretation of our final picture, on the vessel- stand (Plate 8), brings us back to an earlier topic: for once again it has been argued that the central scene represents the truce after Ajax and Hector’s single combat in the Iliad. Once again, I suggest, we can only accept it if we utterly disregard the inappropriate context which the artist has provided—the presence of two women, and of a hunter with game, on the batdefield at Troy—and only if we admit the logical underpinning of the identification, namely that the two warriors still duelling further round to the right are the same pair, Ajax and Hector, shown at the immediately preceding stage of the story.
