As noted above, the economic motive in this asymmetrical relationship was great. The calls on the people’s surplus sustained the basileis materially as well as symbolically. Gift-giving among the Homeric elite, by contrast, has maximum social and political purpose, but little economic pur­ pose. Gifts symbolize the relationship. Each gift-act is a product both of what is appropriate and

customary for the occasion and of other variables such as age and position. All offers, acceptances, or ex­ changes of dSra are instrumental, either in establishing, maintaining, or repairing a relationship, or in minimizing hostility, or validating or calibrating (and even creating) differences in rank. Honor and prestige are the bottom line of gift transactions. In every case, the ‘text’ of the gift—who gives what to whom, and why, and how much and in what way—may be read as a public declara­ tion of the relative social ranking of the participants at that moment (IL 11.123-25; Od. 2.184— 86). The emphasis on competition and display in Homeric gift-giving might seem exaggerated, had we not numerous parallels from big-man and chieftain societies world-wide. The guest-friend relationship between foreigners (xeinoi), which is totally free of that kind of rivalry, presents an ideal reciprocity. The host’s hospitality, kind intentions, and parting gift are guaranteed a per­ fectly symmetrical return, with no time limit on the obligation.29 To talk further about gift-behavior would lead into a discussion of 57 DmSer. 11 21.448-49; Od 10.84-85; dmoai: IL 1.112-15; 6.450-58; 12.433-35; Od. 1.356-58; 6.52-53; 20.105-10. 2B See Raaflaub (this vol.). 25 Donlan (1989a) 6-10; Herman (1987). 664 WALTER DONLAN elite power relations. I will concentrate on the material and eco­ nomic aspects. The material of elite gift transactions belongs to a separate form of wealth, ‘treasure,' which was available in a socially useful quantity only to the elite, and circulated exclusively among them.30 Anthropologists know many such ‘multi-centric economies,’ in which social-symbolic wealth circulates in a separate sphere of exchange marked by a ‘different institutionalization and different moral values.’31 Treasure in Homer consists mainly of artifacts of metal or cloth and unworked metal (chiefly gold and iron), the generic word for which is keimelia, ‘things stored up,’ indicating their essential nature— small items, easily transported and stored. The value of treasure goods lies in their scarcity and costliness: embroidered and dyed textiles, bronze arms and armor, gold and silver cups and ornaments, gold and (occasionally) iron in their natural states. Only doth goods, which in fact make up a considerable portion of keimelia, are produced in the oikos; the rest are spedalist manufactures. Among the most valu­ able keimelia are large, unused bronze cauldrons and tripod caul­ drons, utilitarian objects elevated to purely symbolic wealth. Women and horses circulate along with treasure-gifts, since both are highest-

status possessions and both produce keimelia, women with their weav­ ing, and horses as prize-winners in races. The scarcity of treasure is inadvertently emphasized in the epics. Whereas in transactions involving animals the numbers given are very high, treasure-gifts are on a much smaller scale. £ven when the poet wishes to give the impression of an enormous quantity of pres­ tige goods, clearly exaggerating reality, the actual count is rather modest. Most treasure transactions in Homer, in fact, consist of only one to three items.32 The same high numerical and value ratios between animals and keimelia are observed in the few instances where actual equivalencies are given. A large tripod is Vorth’ twelve cattle, an embossed cauldron is ‘worth an ox,’ a splendid silver bowl is equivalent to three horses and a chariot (II. 23.702-703, 884; Od. 4.600-619). It is likely that the quickening economic tempo in the ninth cen- ttiry reflects mainly the growing appetite of the elite for metal and 30 Finley (1978) 61-62, 120-23. 31 E.g., Bohannon (1959). 31 Donlan (1981) 102-103. THE HOMERIC ECONOMY 665 prestige items for purposes of display and gift-giving. That require­ ment for success, amply documented by archaeology and the epics, spurred ambitious oikoi to increase their agricultural and animal surpluses, providing the stimulus for the spiraling growth in the crafts and trading sectors in the eighth and seventh centuries.33 Although ordinary families were not involved directly in the prestige economy, they bore a share of the expense, as Homer shows. It is quite pos­ sible, then, that during the ninth century chieftains were already plac­ ing greater demands on the surplus of their constituents, prompting them to increase their productivity. Wealth in animals, treasure, and female slaves is intimately tied to the institutions of war and raiding, the surest paths to personal glory and to riches in the epics. Since force of arms is the most honorable way to come into possession of these, we may suspect Homer of a selective focus. Even so, we cannot doubt that throughout the Geo­ metric period the raid (which in the Homeric world is a cousin to trade; Od. 3.71-74 = 9.252-55; cf. Thuc. 1.5) was an important economic activity, and that the attacks on poleis (where the keimelia lay), were partly motivated by lust for treasure and women, whatever the other reasons for enmity. The system fostered the continuing dominance of the current

chiefly families, who were the organizers, leaders, and principal beneficiaries of raiding, and were already rich in flocks, and already possessed the nucleus of a raiding party in their ‘retainers’ (theraponles) and ‘close companions’ (philoi hetaxroi). So, while those below them might wish to emulate them, acquisition and maintenance of a large surplus of animals, especially the luxury animals, cattle and horses, was usually possible only for the estab­ lished elite.34 Summary and Conclusions Homer describes an economy that is extremely simple as a functioning system, yet is fairly complex in its relationships, which are socially and ideologically constructed. In Homer, social concerns drive eco­ nomic behavior. The leaders do not direct the economy; basileis in Homer have limited redistributive functions, and do not levy regular M Austin and Vidal-Naquet (1977) 54-56; Starr (1992) 46-49, 61. w The ‘Cretan’ Odysseus is one who did rise to chieftain status: Od. 14.199-234. 666 WALTER DONLAN taxes and dues on the people. There is every indication in Homer that the ‘compliance costs’ to the demos for obeying the chiefs’ demands for gifts are low. The practice of equal shares in the booty and the feast, with something extra for the leaders, is the paradigm of eco­ nomic relations in general. The need to consume animals and treasure to win a good reputation and create obligations operates at every level of leadership and is heaviest on the top ranks. This competition appears inefficient from the perspective of modern economic rationality, but makes perfect sense to the Homeric basileis, who like low-level chiefs everywhere, amass only to spend.35 The system apparently slowed the increase of wealth differentiation, which is relatively unmarked for most of the Dark Age and becomes really severe only in the eighth century. As I suggested earlier, little of the systemic economic changes that occurred between the end of the ninth and the early seventh centu­ ries is found in the Iliad and Odyssey. These include, most notably, the switch from large-scale stock-raising by the elite and their trans­ formation into an agricultural gentry with restrictive access to the land, and the erosion of the ancient principles of leader-people reci­ procity, but also the waning of the animal raid as a major economic activity and the much heavier engagement of the aristocrats in organ­ ized international trade. What precipitated these and a host of other fundamental new developments, such as the ‘decline’

of the para­ mount basileus and the rise of dty-state institutions, war for territory, and a remarkable artistic flowering, including the ‘invention’ of the Greek alphabet and the spread of writing36—all of which were com­ ing to be during ‘Homer’s’ own lifetime—remains a mystery. The economic and social system that epic preserves supposes a ‘back­ ground’ world of much open land, given over mainly to large roving flocks and herds, and isolated sctdcments, both easy prey for maraud­ ing bands. It is people who are scarce in Homer. As soon as the land-to-people ratio began to be reversed (i.e., well before there was any serious strain on the carrying capacity of the land), the old system, which was completely maladapted to the new conditions, challenges, and opportunities, had to change. It is not surprising, therefore, that the ‘structural revolution’ in Greece was accomplished in the relatively short span of three or four generations; nor that the poet’s audiences, living in a society in transition, could still compre­ hend that vanishing background world. Daitz’s readings of the Iliad (Gymnasium 101 p994] 359-60), HOMERIC WARFARE 669 The Heroic Army: Warrior Bands and eTribal3 Contingent The story begins with a red herring: the order of battle as described in the famous Catalogue of Ships. Here the Greek army is drawn up in 29 contingents, varying in size but most commonly comprising about 2,000 men—that is, 40 ships, each with a crew of 50—recruited from a region embracing on average half a dozen cities. The Boiotians are stationed on the right wing (2.526), the Magnesians on the left, and Odysseus’ Kephallenians hold the centre. The Trojans and their allies are similarly divided into 16 contingents according to their places of origin (2.484-877). This would seem a natural enough arrangement. Homer, however, treats the separation of ‘national’ contingents as an unusual notion, and he fails to sustain it, On the Greek side, the division of the troops is first proposed by Nestor: Separate

the men by tribes, by phratries, Agamemnon, so that a phratry may bring aid to phratries, and a tribe to tribes. If you were to act thus and the Greeks would obey you, then you might find out who among the leaders is a coward, and who is a brave man, for they would be fighting amidst their own people (2.362-66). This is presented as a novel and excellent idea (2.370-74); Agamemnon and his closest allies personally take charge of putting it into action (2.439-46, 474-77). The surprising implication is that members of such (pseudo-) kinship groups do not fight as units as a matter of course: they would normally be found scattered across the battle­ field. Meanwhile in Troy, it is pointed out to Hektor that his many allies all speak different languages. ‘Let each man give orders to those whom indeed he leads, and, having drawn up his countrymen, let him lead them out’ (2.803-806). The implication is that until then, forces of different ethnic origins had merged into a single, undivided army. It might be objected that this is an over-literal interpretation, that Homer is merely for dramatic effect introducing as a fresh inven­ tion a form of organization which must have been commonplace. Yet when we turn to the battle narrative, we find in fact no trace of distinct contingents and every indication that die troops mingle at will. When on occasion the poet indicates the location of certain bodies of men on the battlefield, their positions do not remotely match those in the Catalogue (e.g., 4.251-421; 13.685-708). This is hardly surpris­ ing, since their leaders are extremely mobile. Hektor, having retired hurt from the centre of the battlefield (11.354-60), is next seen fight- 670 HANS VAN WEES ing ‘on the left’ (11,498) until advised to return to his previous posi­ tion (11.523-42). A different principle of military organization is assumed throughout the narrative, although never explicitly described, and this is much more easily reconciled with the mobility of the heroes: networks of personal ties unite the army, giving it a loose and flexible structure. The two key terms defining personal relations in the army are the egalitarian ‘companion’ (hetairos) and the hierarchical ‘follower’ (therapdrv, literally ‘attendant’). Everyone in the army is thought of as everyone else’s ‘companion,’3 though some are inevitably closer companions than others. Being a follower, on the other hand, is neither a mutual nor a general relation, but involves one man’s subordination to another. Meriones, say, follows Idomeneus and no one else. The men who form a contingent are simultaneously their commander’s follow­ ers and his companions: thus the Myrmidons are variously described as Akhilleus’ ‘dose-fighting theroporOei (16.272; 17.165) and as his hetairoi (e.g., 1.179-80). Within the contingent, though, distinctions are drawn between dose personal followers and more distant ones, some of whom may have followers of their own. Some special ties of companion­ ship may even cut across contingents. Small, fluid groups constituted by the dosest of these relationships operate as units on and off the battlefield. HOMERIC WARFARE 673 It is impossible to tell, however, how many companions are sup­ posed to be at their leader’s side at any particular moment. Some­ times it seems that most of his contingent is with him; at other times, perhaps only his own band, or only a few of his closest friends. What happens in the course of battle is apparently a constant splitting, recombining, and temporary merging of groups. Take the Cretan contingent, which is clearly split into at least two parts when, as we have seen, Idomeneus and his follower Meriones are fighting in differ­ ent parts of the frontline. Idomeneus subsequently leaves the batde- field with a number of companions—presumably no more than half a dozen—to carry a wounded comrade to safety (13.210-15); Meriones also leaves the battlefield, probably with a few companions of his own, although these are not mentioned (13.162-68). Both thus con­ tribute to dividing further whatever parts of the Cretan army had been fighting with them. Then they team up and decide to rejoin the men left behind by Idomeneus, thereby reconstituting at least part of the contingent. We shall later come across examples of sizable groups merging when their leaders decide to join forces for a while. In combat, then, the heroic army knows no cohesive and exclu­ sive military units; accordingly, there is no technical term either for ‘warrior band’ or ‘contingent,’ and the latter can only be described in a roundabout way as an aggregate of ‘tribes and phratries.’7 In­ stead, battle is conducted by mobile and changing clusters of war­ riors, based on ties of companionship and personal subordination. Leaders and their closest followers form small but relatively stable cores which expand and contract as other followers and friends join or leave. How­ ever, Homeric Greek appears to be as unspecific as modem English is in its use of these words, and both the image of a ‘cloud’ of sol­ diers and the spontaneous pressing together of the crowd when it is fired up suggest, not a neat formation, but an amorphous mass.9 That it is the men of Akhilleus and Aias who are depicted in this manner is no coincidence, for they are elsewhere singled out as the two bravest contingents (8.224— 26, 11.7-9): densely massed troops are clearly the Homeric ideal. Several times, a body of soldiers is divided by its commander into five sections. Akhilleus ‘appointed five leaders to whom he entrusted the giving of orders... and he placed all men around the leaders, dividing them well’ (16.171-72, 198-99); Nestor, too, draws up his followers ‘around’ five named men (4.293-96). In preparation for an assault on the Greek camp the whole Trojan army spontaneously regroups: ‘taking separate stations, packing themselves together, or­ dered in five groups, they followed their leaders’ (12.86-87). A few other passages also hint at fivefold divisions.10 Like the contingents, these sections play no part in the battle itself, except that the Tro­ jans retain them for the duration of their assault on the Greek wall, and only resume their usual mobility after they have broken through. Unlike the contingents, however, no special advice is needed to cre­ ate sections, and there is no suggestion that they are meant to be permanent units. Perhaps it is understood that such subdivisions are a common but temporary feature of military formations. They might be specifically designed to give added cohesion to the troops during the advance, but not intended to stay intact in battle. Certainly the cohesion of their forces during the advance is a major concern for Homeric commanders. Akhilleus’ men represent the ideal: ‘immediately they swarmed out like wasps... and in their masses fell upon the Trojans’ (16.259, 276). Nevertheless, the first breakthrough follows immediately. It occurs at noon when a bolt of lightning strikes panic into the Greeks, who take to flight (8.68-79). The third and longest battle narrative describes the initial dash almost as briskly, and just as abruptly juxtaposes images of close- range and missile combat. ‘Trojans

and Greeks leapt at one another, and killed... The fight was evenly balanced, and they raged like wolves... For as long as it was morning... missiles from both sides hit their mark, and men fell,’ until at lunchtime, ‘the Greeks by their own prowess broke the enemy forces’ (11.70-73, 84-85, 90-91). The fourth and final battle involves no initial clash at all, but turns into a rout from the very start, so frightened are the Trojans of Akhilleus (20.41-46). The problem with these opening scenes is one that occurs in many later episodes as well. They appear to combine in an awkward manner three distinct elements—open order combat by promakhoi, dose order hand-to-hand fighting, and mass exchanges of missiles. HOMERIC WARFARE 679 Scholars have offered a range of solutions. The epic tradition may have incorporated two historically distinct styles of warfare: an older, Dark Age form in which promakhoi fight while the mass stands well back hurling missiles, and a more recent form in which the mass does all the fighting, at close range and in dense formation.13 An­ other theory is that only the massed fighting is historical, while promakhoi- style combat is a poetic fantasy, superimposed upon it to enhance the narrative, and perhaps reflecting the imagery associated with heroes in cult.14 1 5 Both views are tenable, if we are willing to believe that contemporary audiences were capable of suspending disbelief to the extent of not being offended by bold juxtapostions of types of warfare which they must have known from experience were incompatible. The alternative is to assume that Homer’s audience would have expected something, not wholly realistic, but more plausible and more like the battles fought by themselves. The answer may then lie in distinguishing phases within battle: perhaps a phase of missile war­ fare first, then a period of promakhoi combat, followed by massed hand- to-hand in the closing stages.13 Or a massed clash first, during which the formations eventually disintegrate and space opens up for missile fighting and skirmishing by promakhoi.16 The drawback of this approach is that neither sequence quite matches the course of events in all four episodes, and that there is no indication of any transition between phases. It is perhaps conceivable that the poet presents an abrupt short-hand version of successive stages of battle, but this would be unusual in a narrative which is normally quite expansive. Moreover, when

Homer tells us who was ‘first’ to kill his man (4.457), he is much more likely to be speaking of the beginning of battle than of the beginning of skirmishing after a sustained massed assault has fizzled out 13 A traditionally widespread view, see, e.g., G. Murray (1907) 151; Webster (1958) 214— 20. More recently, H. Singor ([1995] 193-99; cf. [1991]) adds the suggestion that the earliest forms of close order hand-to-hand fighting appearing alongside the older form of combat consist of a small number of aristocratic warriors forming up in a single line. '« Thus Pritchett (1991) 181-90; (1985) 21-30; similarly Lang (1910) 51-59. 680 HANS VAN WEES Finally, it is possible that the confusion is all in our minds. We may be jumping to conclusions when we take ‘shields clashing’ as a reference to massed close combat, or 'missiles flying’ as a reference to mass long range combat. An audience familiar with the kind of warfare in which the bulk of the army keeps its distance from the enemy, as in the very first encounter, would not expect any battle to open with massed hand-to-hand fighting, and would therefore under­ stand the clashing shields and flying spears as those of numerous promakhoi, ‘leaping forward’ and ‘raging like wolves’ in mobile, open- order combat. If so, all batdes begin in the same style of combat by promakhoi, described sometimes in close-up, sometimes in panoramic sweep, with varying emphasis on handweapons or missiles. This style continues until a breakthrough is achieved.17 If we are prepared to accept its premises regarding audience expectations of the consist­ ency of the narrative and the nature of battle, this is an economical explanation. Flight, pursuit and rally A breakthrough in battle is often attributed to divine intervention, but on the human plane it is achieved either by collective effort, or by a single conspicuous killing. We are told that men have been known to win battles which they had been fated to lose, ‘relying on their strength, effort, bravery, and numbers’ (17.328-30); that ‘the Greeks through their own prowess broke the enemy ranks, calling out to their companions

across the lines’ (11.90-91). Yet we are also told that ‘all the Greeks were miraculously put to flight by Hektor and Father Zeus. Hektor killed only one man, Periphetes the Myce­ naean’ (17.636-38), and that ‘Aias, son of Telamon, bulwark of the Greeks, was the first to break a Trojan rank. He brought relief to his companions by hitting the man who had proved to be the best of the Thracians’ (6.5-7). The selectivity of Homer’s narrative must be borne in mind, of course, and a look at its context will show that a decisive individual feat tends to occur when the winning side is enjoying collective success as well, but still the impact of such angle killings is remarkable, and surely unrealistic. 17 Thus van Wees (1994) 2 9; (1988) 2-14; similarly Kromayer and Veith (1928) 22-26. For discussions of these last three views: Gartledge (forthcoming); Snodgrass (1993b); Wheeler (1991) 126-28. HOMERIC WARFARE 681 The beginning of a rout is usually dearly marked by Homer, both by phrases such as ‘the Greeks made the Trojans give way’ (5.37) and by indications that the character of the fighting has changed. Killings no longer alternate between the sides, but become a massacre of one side by the other, often indicated by a catalogue of how ‘each of the leaders killed a man* (5.37-38). The victims normally put up no resistance. They tend to be mounting their chariots, or already mounted and turning around, as they try to escape, and they are often hit in the back. ‘First Agamemnon, lord of men, hurled out of his chariot the great Odios, leader of the Halizones, who was the first to turn. He planted a spear in his back between the shoulders and drove it out through his chest5 (5.38-41). Sometimes, there is a spate of killings of men in pairs, who are presumably thought of as warriors and their charioteers, caught trying to flee.18 The slaughter during pursuit is not always a wholly one-sided affair, but the gen­ eral pattern is unmistakable. O f course the fleeing troops lose all cohesion and are scattered far and wide. In one instance, when the Trojans breach the wall around the camp, a large body of Greeks runs all the way back to their ships, and just sit there, tired and tearful, ‘reviving their spirits,’ while some of their comrades are still trying to resist (13.83-89).

Nor do the pursuers attempt to maintain formation. The close Trojan ranks drawn up before the assault on the wall evaporate as soon as they are successful: ‘now that they have surmounted the wall, some of the Trojans remain standing at a distance with their weapons, and others fight scattered among the ships, a few against many’ (13.737-39). Two factors aggravate the disintegration of the troops, first, leaders taking to their chariots, including the conscientious Hektor, appear to flee and pursue as fast as they can, inevitably leaving behind their followers on foot: ‘the fast horses carried Hektor and his weapons away, and he left the men of Troy,5 who found their way blocked by a trench (16.367-69). Second, during pursuit, men take their time to plunder the corpses of the dead, which not only leads to further scattering of the troops, but also severely slows down the pursuit and gives the enemy a chance to get away. Accordingly, commanders try telling their men to concentrate on the chase and leave the spoils for later (6.67-71; 15.347). IB See Willcock (1993). 682 HANS VAN WEES In these conditions it is possible for small groups to rally and create pockets of resistance. In staging a rally, individual heroes seem again remarkably effective. For instance, simply by standing their ground and killing a few men while all the other Greeks are still fleeing, Odysseus and Diomedes seem able to balance the battle (11.310- 336). In the next line, however, it is suddenly revealed that there are other Greeks present (337), and we must conclude that these and other ‘lone’ defenders are accompanied by their followers, just as Aias turned out to be when, as we have seen, he appeared to hold back the entire Trojan army by himself. It must not be forgotten, moreover, that such individual rallies restore the balance only in one part of the front, though sometimes they can have a snowballing effect when others join in: ‘“Friends, leaders and lords of the Greeks, turn round, stand your ground, and save Aias, who is being over­ come by missiles...”’ Thus spoke the wounded Eurypylos, and the others came and stood close by him, leaning their shields against their shoulders and raising their spears’ (11.587-94). Army-wide rallies, by contrast, do not result from individual hero­ ics but occur when the troops reach a defensible place, such as trench, wall, or

ships, and spontaneously make a stand, or when a leader, ranging across the army and haranguing all the troops, inspires a renewed collective effort.19 When this happens, the scattered forces regroup. The original gap between the armies is restored, the chari­ ots which had gone ahead in pursuit fall back to rejoin the footsoldiers, and some of the cohesion of the original formation is regained. Immediately, Hektor in his armor jumped down from his chariot and, shaking his sharp spears, he went everywhere among the army with exhortations to fight... They turned round and stood facing the Greeks. (5.494— 97; 6.103-106) The Greeks retreated and stopped the slaugh­ ter. (6.107) The Greeks held their ground in droves and were not afraid... They turned white in the shower of dust kicked up among them... by the hooves of the horses which rejoined them, for the charioteers turned them round. (5.498-505) 19 Latacz (1977) 96 115, which is much more persuasive than the interpretation of mass movements as an arbitrary pattern dependent on the presumed literary conventions of the so-called aristao of individual heroes suggested by Krischer (1971) 13-89. HOMERIC WARFARE 683 Intensification of battle After a successful rally, regular ‘standing’ combat (stadie husmine) is resumed, until the next breakthrough occurs. Although the forces have regrouped, they can no longer be arranged in a regular rank- and-file structure—if they ever were. Rallies being by nature impro­ vised and hurried, one would expect the troops to remain in a rather chaotic and scattered state, and the evidence suggests that indeed they did. Throughout the ensuing battle scenes, the men clearly enjoy great freedom of movement, not only, as we have seen, across the front line, but also from front line to camp or city and back again. Hav­ ing staged a rally, Hektor walks back to Troy (6.103-118), and when he later returns with Paris, the two of them instantly move through the army right up to the front, where each kills a man (7.1- 12). Deiphobos retreats from the front to the back of the crowd, to find Aeneas and lead him to the front again (13.455-69). When Hektor is wounded, he either manages to run back to his chariot and then drive further away from the front ‘into the mass’ (11.354—60 ), or he is carried to his chariot which then removes him from the batdefield altogether (14.428-39). The wounded and

dead are often helped to safety in this way. Since there is apparently always space for men and chariots to move through, the formation of the mass must be imagined as remaining fairly open during these stages of battle. At the front, the intensity of batde tends to fluctuate over time, and to differ markedly from one part of the line to the next. Thus, during the fight over the corpse of Patroklos: The other Trojans and Greeks did battle in comfort, under a dear sky... They fought intermittently, avoiding one another’s pain-inflict­ ing missiles, standing far apart. But those in the center suffered griev­ ously ... For them a great fight of painful rivalry developed all day. The sweat of exhaustion constandy, relendessly streamed into the eyes and down the arms of those who fought, and down their knees and shins and feet below... All the time with their shaip spears relent­ lessly they dashed forward and killed one another. (17.370-75, 384— 87, 412-13) What causes the intensification of battle is almost always either the need to recover a fallen comrade’s dead body, or the need to help a comrade in danger. This may be achieved in two ways: either by bringing together forces from different parts of the front and concen- 684 HANS VAN WEES trating them in one spot, or by calling upon men who have been hanging back to come to the front. An example of the first method is the appeal by Menelaos to the ‘leaders and lords’ for help in saving the corpse of Patroklos: ‘Aias son of Oileus heard him clearly and was the first to come towards him, running through the fighting, and after him Idomeneus and Meriones ... Who could name in his mind the names of the rest, all those Greeks behind them who roused batde?’ (17.246-61) In an instance of bringing help to a comrade in danger, the poet spells out what is no doubt implied elsewhere, that the anonymous multitude includes followers as well as leaders. Aineias asks Deiphobos, Paris, and Agenor to stand by him, and we are told: They were leaders of the Trojans together with him, but their men followed after them... Aineias rejoiced in his heart when he saw the crowd of men follow­ ing behind him’ (13.489-95). The second method can be equally effective. At one stage, Poseidon, in the guise of the

seer Kalkhas, intervenes to reinforce a rally being staged by the Aiantes. He stirs up the troops who have given up on the fight and are sitting dispiritedly by the ships. Going amongst them, he easily encouraged the strong ranks [phalanges]. He went first to Teukros and Leitos, exhorting them, and to die hero Peneleos, and to Thoas, Deipyros, Meriones and Antilokhos ... Thus exhorting them, Poseidon spurred on the Greeks. Strong ranks went and stood around the two Aiantes..., for the chosen best men stood their ground against the Trojans and Hektor, forming a fence with spear against spear and shield against shield. (13.89-93, 125-30) This is followed by the lines also used to describe Akhilleus’ troops pressing together before battle, with the additional observation that ‘brandished in brave hands, spears overlapped’ (13.131-35). Although a more select group than Aineias’ supporters, this is still clearly a large and dense crowd consisting of more than merely the nine lead­ ers actually named. It is by no means unusual to find warriors needing encouragement to join combat. On the contrary, at any moment during battle there are always those who choose to keep out of the fighting, because they are tired or scared, or because they hold a grudge against their leader (13.107-110, 459-61; 14.49-51). Hektor himself spends some of his time in the rear, when he is advised not to fight as promakhos but to ‘wait among the multitude and out of the turmoil’ (20.376- 77). Men in general may ‘shirk the fighting of their own free will’ HOMERIC WARFARE 685 (13.234) or ‘stand off and fight not, doing as they please’ (14.132). It is accordingly a major part of a leader’s task to motivate as many men as possible to join battle rather than hang back, and appeals to stop ‘shirking’ are constantly addressed to both individuals and soldiers at large. ‘Shall we shirk like this, Melanippos?... Follow me! We can no longer fight the Greeks from a distance’ (15.553-57). ‘Do not stand far away from the Trojans now, you Greeks. Come! A man must go forward against another, and be eager to fight’ (20.354-55).20 Whether by concentrating active troops or by mobilizing those who have remained passive, assembling a dense formation is presented as a highly effective defensive tactic. The men gathered round the Aiantes, ‘tightly pressing together, like a wall’ (13.152), check the seemingly unstoppable advance of

Hektor: ‘when he ran into these dense ranks, he came to a halt very close by. The Greeks facing him struck at him with swords and spears, and pushed him away from them; he was shaken, and drew back’ (13.145-48). The troops assembled in defence of the body of Patroklos have an even greater impact: Asteropaios went forward, he too being eager to fight the Greeks, but that was no longer at all possible. For standing around Patroklos, they enclosed him on all sides with their shields, and held out their spears before them. For Aias went round everywhere with constant exhorta­ tions; he urged that no one should retreat behind the corpse, and that no one should fight as promakhos, standing out from the other Greeks.... The earth was drenched with purple blood and crowded together lay the dead bodies of both Trojans and proud allies—and of Greeks, for they did not fight a bloodless battle. Yet far fewer of the Greeks were killed, for in the crowd they always remembered to protect one another’s fives. (17.352-65) It is significant that it is the Greeks who are most successful in apply­ ing these tactics. Their superior solidarity and co-operative obedience are highlighted elsewhere, too (3.2-9; 4.428-38). Aias’ creation of a totally cohesive body of troops is emphatically represented as the best way to stage a defence, but it is equally emphatically exceptional. In no other fight is anyone actually forbid­ den to leave the formation; nowhere else is it said that it is impossible for one of the enemy to attack the formation by himself; and in no other episode is a massing of troops in fact followed by an extended scene of intense mass combat without any reference to individual 20 See van Wees (1988) 12-14. 686 HANS VAN WEES heroics (17.366-425). Troops may mass together in other crises, but even when the Trojans renew their assault on the SvalT of men around the Aiantes, or later when they charge at the ships, which the Greeks have ‘surrounded with a fence of bronze’ (15.566-67), the fighting which immediately ensues always implies a certain distance between the opposing formations, and involves men running forward, throw­ ing missiles, and retreating, in the usual proma/chos-style. It would appear that Aias’ tactics are unique in leading to a phase of massed hand-to-hand combat, confined to the center of the line (17.370-83), and

ending when a new crisis develops elsewhere (17.426-542). At all other times, despite the gathering of dense masses, men continue to be mobile and to fight in open order.21 Again, then, we are faced with an apparent contrast between massed and individual action, and with a range of possible solutions similar to the ones suggested for the initial clashes. Perhaps Homer juxta­ poses the individualism of Dark Age warriors, or of poetic fancy, with the solidarity and discipline of contemporary armies. If so, we might wonder not only at the audience’s capacity for suspending disbelief, but also at the way in which Homer on the one hand al­ ways integrates massed formations into the narrative through explicit descriptions of how they are created, and on the other hand always abruptly reverts to individual combat without any explanation. This peculiarity of the narrative casts some doubt also on the alternative view that Homeric battles proceed in distinct phases.22 What is more, it is hard to account for the extreme rarity of actual descriptions of massed close combat, which on this view is the decisive stage of battle. One would have to assume that after the account of the build-up of troops the phase of massed combat itself is either simply skipped (as being unsuitable for poetic treatment, perhaps) or else is in fact recounted but frequently spoiled by inappropriate references to promakhos-style individual mobility and the use of missiles. When the fight over the body of Patroklos is resumed after the diversion of 17.426-342, the narrative docs feature individual heroes, promakhoi, individual mo­ bility, and the use of missiles (17.574-92); apparently the cohesion imposed by Aias has vanished. For a detailed discussion of passages featuring promakhoi-style combat immediately after a tightening of formations, see van Wees (1988) 7-10, but ignore the strained attempt to explain away Aias’ exceptional tactics. n The narrative offers no support for the suggestion that the transition to massed fighting is achieved by promakhm returning to their place in the ranks of a massed formation (which had been standing at the ready while they were skirmishing) and giving the order to advance (Latacz [1977] 171-78; Albracht [1886] 39). HOMERIC WARFARE 687 The remaining possibility is that we are once more jumping to conclusions when we assume that a massing together of troops is necessarily designed to lead to collective hand-to-hand combat. If, as suggested, Homer’s audiences did

not imagine the initial clash of armies to be anything but an encounter of numerous individual pro- makhoi, with the bulk of the army keeping its distance, then it is probable that they would not have expected a renewed build-up of troops to result in a massed dash either. Instead, they may have assumed that a densdy-packed formation would merely serve as a solid defensive line and not only provide a concentration of potential promakhoi, but also give these men greater confidence to attack in the knowledge that the ‘crowd of companions’ to fall back on or call upon for help is now larger and closer at hand. This would again account for the evidence quite economically, provided one is willing to accept that, although the Iliad recognizes and indeed recommends the possibility of pushing the cohesion of the ranks beyond this, into actual massed combat, it is nevertheless accomplished only once, locally and temporarily, due to one leader’s special initiative in an extreme crisis. The nature o f promakhoi-romiat However we interpret the massed formations, combat by individual promakhoi unquestionably dominates the narrative. Their style of fighting is conventionally described as ‘duelling,’ and in a few of the lenghtier confrontations there may be some justification for this. In the fullest possible sequence, the opponents challenge one another before they each let fly one or two missiles. Then they close in to fight hand-to- hand, and the fight is settled with the first or second blow. The victor may shout boasts or taunts at the enemy, and take spoils. Occasionally he mutilates his victim’s corpse before retreating to the safety of the crowd of companions. This complete sequence, how­ ever, is a hypothetical composite and never actually occurs in the Iliad. Some encounters contain most of its elements, but most con­ tain only a few. A single, instantly fatal spear-cast, for instance, with­ out any run-up or follow-up, is quite common. It is sometimes supposed that the hypothetical full sequence is the norm, and that the shorter encounters are meant to highlight only the decisive moment in it While this is conceivable, it is more likely that even the briefest of sequences represent the full extent of a hero’s 688 HANS VAN WEES intervention in the action. In a fair number of instances, at any rate, it is dear that they do: There Harpalion, son of king Pylaimenes, leapt at

him ... From nearby he then struck with his spear the centre of (Menelaos9 ] shield, but was unable to drive his weapon through it, and withdrew again into the crowd of companions to escape death, looking all round him in case someone would touch his skin with a weapon (13.642-49). In the vast majority of cases, 'hit-and-run attack’ is a much more appropriate label than ‘duel,’ espedally since in pitched battle, as opposed to formal single combat outside it, warriors often opportu­ nistically exploit their chances without any sign of chivalric etiquette.23 Both traditional and more recent interpretations hold that promakkoi are an elite. Traditionally, they have been seen as a small group of aristocratic ‘champions,’ as opposed to the commoners who form the ineffective ‘multitude.’ Lately, with the recognition that the poet constantly implies the presence of many more promakkoi than the handful of heroes mentioned by name, they have come to be seen as a rather broader group, consisting of the most heavily-armed among the warriors, who form the first line or lines of a formation other­ wise composed of less well-equipped men taking part only in the massed fighting.24 These views are just about compatible with the evidence, if we assume that appeals for help and exhortations to stop shirking, despite being addressed to “you Greeks’ or ‘you Trojans’ in general, are intended only for members of the elite, and if, more­ over, we assume that only the higher-ranking or better-equipped of the heroes’ followers and companions actually join them in combat It is quite conceivable, however, that exhortations to come and join battle at the front are indeed addressed to the entire mass. One passage in particular can hardly be explained any other way: ‘They rebuked whomever they saw shirking the fight completely: ‘Triends, you who are outstanding among the Greeks, you who are average, and 19 See Mueller (1984) 81-82, for the view that Homer selects for description the final, decisive blow only. In the light of this appeal, we should also take seriously the claim made by Thersites, the ‘worst’ man in the army (2.248) and a ‘man of the common people’ (2.198), that he and his like in fact bear the brunt of the fighting (2.231, 235-38). It would certainly be physically possible for anyone present on the battlefield to join com­ bat actively. The openness of the formation, which allows the heroes to move anywhere along the front and through the mass, would equally allow any member of the crowd to come forward and join the promakhoi for a while, if he so chose. Nor need the poorer men’s lack of armor be a hindrance, for besides suggesting that the possession of helmets, shields, and greaves is widespread, Homer shows unar­ mored archers operating in the front line, either independently (3.16— 20) or in co-operation with a heavy-armed warrior (8.266-72). If it is true that anyone in the mass is eligible to fight at the front, it would mean that the distinction between promakhoi and ‘multitude’ is merely a topographical one. Among the promakhoi would be reck­ oned anyone, from famous hero to anonymous commoner, who is currently fighting at the front; among the ‘multitude’ at any particu­ lar time are all those who are currently out of action, including lead­ ing heroes temporarily retired from the fray. Promakhoi-comhat, on this view, would be a form of mass (not massed) fighting, both in the sense that numerous men fight simultaneously, and every man in the army is called upon to take his turn in the frontline, and in the sense that the common ‘masses’ play a major role in it. Historical Implications It has often been said that Homer, as a poet, cannot necessarily be expected to be consistent in his account, all the more so since he inherited a long oral tradition liable to contain material from more than one historical period. This is true, and it is therefore possible that the battle narrative is, as often claimed, a mixture of incompat­ ible elements. On the other hand, a poet

who has a clear mental image of what he is describing may very well produce a consistent narrative, even without consciously trying to, while oral traditions are often quite adaptable and may contain very little that is not new or updated. So it is equally possible that the Iliad might contain an internally coherent picture of heroic warfare, and indeed of the he­ roic world. 690 Hans van wees It has been suggested here that we can in fact reconstruct an al­ most wholly consistent picture of Homeric armies and battles. The heroic army is composed of many small and loosely oiganized bands of warriors, held together by personal des of subordinadon and com­ panionship. Battles are fought in open order, at any particular moment the majority of men remain at a distance from the enemy, while a substantial minority of individual ‘front-line warriors’ venture closer to fight with missiles or hand-to-hand. There is much mobility back and forth as every man in the army is expected to join combat at least occasionally, and even the bravest heroes redre from battle every so often. This picture of warfare accounts for the greater part of the narrative, and is plausible in itself: parallels may be found in ‘primi­ tive’ warfare.25 Homer, however, goes beyond this simple image in three respects. His story adds heavy armor, chariots, and massed formations. None of these features is necessarily incompatible with the rest of the pic­ ture, as has been shown, but some would argue that their Homeric usage as reconstructed here is inefficient and therefore implausible. Heavy armor is far from ideal for the heroes’ mobile style of fight­ ing. Chariots are most effectively used in groups, and as mobile plat­ forms to fight from, rather than singly, as transport to and from battle. Massed formations are better employed in collective close combat than as a base for individual hit-and-run sallies. The answer to these objections must be that optimum efficiency is not by any means the only criterion governing the conduct of war­ fare. Heavy equipment may slow a man down, and confine him to relatively short bursts of activity, but the protection, and even the prestige, gained by wearing costly bronze armor may well have counted for more.26 Its twin roles of status symbol and means of escape would have encouraged the use of the chariot, but at the same time the

value of the horses may have inclined their owners to keep them out of the actual fighting, while the fact that each of these owners leads a band of footsoldiers would have prevented them from teaming up as a separate chariot battalion.27 The need for solidarity in combat may have been felt keenly enough to make a 25 Parallels: van Wees (1986) 296-97 (organization) (1994) 1, 8 (style of fighting). M For recent discussions of further problems associated with Homeric arms and armor, see, e.g., the volumes Kriegswesen in Archaeotogia Homerica EJ (1977), E2 (1980); van Wees (1994) 131-40. 27 Further discussion of chariots in Homer. Van Wees (1994) 9-13, 140-41. Note HOMERIC WARFARE 691 local and temporary massing of troops for defensive purposes fea­ sible, but the loose and informal structure of the Homeric army would in all probability have failed to provide the organizational discipline required to maintain this cohesion in combat, let alone to extend it to the entire army and for the foil duration of battle. If all these elements of the heroic picture are mutually compatible and their combination not implausible, it would follow that two key features of the Classical hoplite phalanx—the bronze panoply and the massed formation—arc already an integral part of Homeric warfare, but that the use made of the formation is as yet much more limited. In the Iliad, we may be witnessing an embryonic hoplite phalanx in the process of development. Indeed, we may be catching a glimpse of how further development was brought about, in Aias’ imposition of an exceptionally cohesive order, a ‘logical’ but not easily accomplished extension of the heroes’ regular tactics, which takes Homeric warfare another step closer to its Classical counterpart. Ongoing military change could also account for the single certain anomaly in the Homeric picture: the contingents introduced at the outset, only to disappear immediately. The notion that allied communities fight best in separate contingents (‘tribes,’ or perhaps groups of tribes), and that formal kinship groups within communities (‘phratries’) ought to fight as distinct units, too, is a radical departure from the indiscriminate mingling, fosing, and fissioning of informally constituted warrior bands encountered everywhere else. It is conceiv­ able but rather unlikely that this conception of ‘tribal’ military orga­ nization is merely a literary conceit created to describe the legendary multinational armies gathered at Troy; at the same time, the care with which it

is introduced and its rationale is explained suggests that it is not a conception that the audience took for granted. W. H. ADKINS We can now propose an approach to the cross-cultural study of values. We shall not be

concerned with a philosophical critique, but with an ‘anthropological’ approach which will show features of the situation which favor the values that we discover and also any inco­ herences in such values which work against the goals that the members of this culture propose to themselves. The study must be of ‘values,’ not of ‘morality:’ if we single out a favored set of values—usually, of course, the set favored by our own community—by terming it the ‘morality’ of the society being studied, there is a danger that much will be overlooked. To treat as the society’s values the whole set of values held to be important by the society—but not necessarily equally important—will be the most illuminating method. One should begin by identifying them, duly noting judgments and evaluations made by the characters and any reason assigned for making them. One should also carefully study the ‘set pieces’ that the poet includes in his work (e.g., Sarpedon’s speech to Glaukos, II. 12.310-28). The reader should note that my use of ‘values’ and ‘goals’ from this point onwards differs from that of most scholars. ‘Values’ is usually employed of the ends which an agent proposes to himself or herself as those he or she intends to pursue, and it is often implied that the only link that binds these values together is that the agent pursues them. I use ‘goals’ in this sense, of such clearly envisioned ends as sacking Troy, creating social harmony, or reducing the national debt. ‘Values,’ on the other hand, signifies the value-judgments which are, or are believed to be, conducive to attaining those goals. If the goal is peace and prosperity, it makes sense to enquire whether the values are indeed appropriate, in that they—usually—conduce to the envi­ sioned goaL They might be contained in such phrases as ‘It is msekron to be defeated,’ ‘strive to make a friend of your enemy,’ and ‘the agathos must fight bravely.’ The subsequent discussion will make it increasingly apparent that the values may not conduce to the attain­ ment of the goals. Agathos, Arete, and Similar Terms We may now begin to study Homeric value-terms in more detail. We shall survey first some scattered passages which employ the words agathos, esthlos, arete, and their contraries kakos, deilos, and kakotes. These words, like most Greek value-terms, are untranslatable. As the most HOMERIC ETHICS 699 powerful terms available to commend or

This use is seen most dearly when Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, claims to be adept at all kinds of menial tasks ‘such as the more kakoi do for the agathoi’ (Od. 15.324). Evidently the military competitive excellences are in the foreground, and we may expect them to take precedence over the quiet coopera­ tive qualities.11 Indeed, only the competitive are spoken of as aretai: the cooperative are not. Given that time denotes the status-conferring goods already held within the oikos of a powerful man, with the addition of those which accrue from later occasions for the distribution of booty, and that the oikos is the locus for the storing and defense of such time, and that the primary function of the agathos is to defend his time with all the resources at his command, it is inevitable that arete and time are two of the most important value-terms to be found in the Homeric poems, and that they are linked to one another. Examination of the usage of other words closely linked with time throws light on this. The importance of time to the Homeric world is made clearer by two verbs derived from the same root: tiein and linein, with its middle form tinesthai. Tiein, a synonym of timan ‘honor,’ denotes the activity of bestowing time on a person, the person being the object of the verb, while tinein denotes the transaction when the time is the object of the verb, something like ‘paying out time,' and tinesthai denotes ‘getting back time for oneself.’ In some usages of 706 A. W. H. ADKINS these words and phrases, there is no particular emphasis on specified material time. This fact suggests that any occasion for moving time in or out of oikoi is conceptualized in the same way: whatever is emphasized in translation, in Homeric Greek its most important feature is to be a transfer of time. Alkinoos can use tinesthai of his intended collection from his subjects to balance the additional valuable gifts which he and his counselors are to give to Odysseus. He seems to have suffi­ cient authority simply to decree that this shall be done. There is a transfer of time, but no-one is punished, although apotinein in other contexts is rendered by ‘be punished.’ Similarly, when Achilles tries to persuade Agamemnon to return Chryseis to her father without asking anything of the Greeks in return, he adds ‘But the Greeks will apotinein threefold or fourfold’ if they capture Troy. Again, no- one is being punished. In Od. 3.195-98, it is said that Aegisthus lapetise miserably... since Orestes

etisatoi’ (Orestes killed him). Both aspects of the transfer of time are mentioned in the one passage. To apotinem timen to a phüos, or one whom one hopes to make into a pkilos, is to enter upon a relationship of reciprocal benefits; to do the same to an enemy is something that one would do only under compulsion, as ‘punishment’ to oneself. In all these examples, a transfer of time is certainly occurring, and it is this which links the usages. This account of the time-group matches the account of the arete- group. Arete in Homer is courage-and-physical-prowess-and-social- position-and-fame. It denotes and commends all these qualities together because the general needs of Homeric society demand that all should be united in certain individuals. The man of arete is the agathos, who necessarily possesses a great many goods and qualities; and he has time, which in some way denotes and commends his position in life. In fact, a man’s time is his position—concretely viewed—on that scale at whose top are the immortal gods, at whose bottom is the wander­ ing beggar. To be deprived of time is to be moved so much nearer to penury and nothingness, sometimes literal death. Small wonder that the response should be so violent. With philotes are associated the adjcctive/noun pftilos and the verb pttilein, and with xenie the nouns HOMERIC ETHICS 707 xeinos and xeinodokos, the adjective phibxeinos and the verb xeinizein/ -izeslhaL All actions and relationships which may be denoted with words from the *xein root may also be denoted with words from the *phil root, but not vice versa. The translation ‘friendship’ is not entirely satisfactory, as will appear. The lexica offer two ‘meanings’ for philos in Homer: ‘own’ and ‘dear.’ They suggest no reason why Homeric language, which has a full set of reflexive pronominal adjectives, should feel the need of pkilos as well; but there are certainly a number of instances in which the translation ‘dear’ appears very strange (to say this is not to say that the remaining instances are correctly and folly translated, simply that the translation causes no problems). If we discuss the usage of these terms in the light of the usage of agathos and arete, time and tinesthai, much will become clear. In our discussion of

the Homeric agathos, his need to defend his oikos and the possessions that it contained became apparent; but no one can defend himself against a hostile or indifferent world by the strength of his right arm alone, however well-armed he may be; and the Homeric hero might well find useful a word whose function was to mark off from the rest of the contents of the world those things and persons on which he can, or should be able to, rely. This is the function of this group of terms. We begin close to the agathos and work outwards. We can begin no closer than parts and aspects of the agathos himself. Phibs can certainly be used of these: ‘But why did my pkilos spirit (thumos) say these things to me?’ (II. 11.407). ‘Their phüa limbs were ‘loosed’ with grievous toil’ (II. 13.85). A translation of either of these phrases that uses either ‘own’ or ‘dear’ will be in a sense comprehensible; but if we compare them with the rest of Homer’s usage of pkilos, what do we imagine that Homer meant? If we move a little further from the agathos, we find 'phila clothing,’ ‘phüa bed,’ pkilos... patridos aies....’ ‘Dear native land’? ‘Own native land’? ‘Own dear native land’? We might give a different answer in different examples. We might dis­ agree. But if we focus on the Greek, it is difficult to suppose that for Homer and his contemporaries there is any difference. Even if we consider only cases where pkilos is applied to persons, there are some puzzles. Oddest of all is the case of Eriphyle, whose shade Odysseus met in the underworld: ‘hateful Eriphyle, who took... gold for contriving the death of her phibs a m ' (Od. 11.326). There is a relevant set-piece, when the Greek Diomedes meets the Lycian Glaukos and, in the conversational manner of the Homeric warrior, asks his identity {II. 6.119-65). Glaukos names his father (Hippolochus) and

his grandfather (Bellerophon). To which Diomedes responds: Then indeed you are a xvinos on my father’s side from olden time; for goodly Oineus entertained blameless Bellerophon in his halls, having kept him there for twenty days. And they supplied one another with fine xeineia, gifts to seal friendship. Diomedes suggests that they avoid one another on the battlefield. Diomedes and Glaukos are unknown to each other; but they are unwilling to fight against one another because of a compact made by their grandfathers. This should not surprise us. The xeinos is the most remote member of the group of persons linked with the ogathos in bonds of reciprocal assistance: his philoi. As he is the most remote, the claim of the xeinos for help is likely to be invoked least often, but to be most urgent when it is invoked, for the xeinos is then least able to defend himself effectively. The xeinos is unlikely to be willing to hazard such advantages for the sake of a transient event such as the Trojan War. It also follows that philotes and xeinie are objective rela­ tionships, not dependent on the emotions of the participants. Amphia- raos was Eriphyle’s pkilos ana, whatever her subsequent feelings for him. To say this is not to say that no Greek experienced any emo­ tion in any relationship of philotes or xeinie; it is to say that emotion was not the common element that bound philoi together. Success in this life may be more or less equated with divine approval, failure with divine anger. Homer’s mortal characters have an urgent practical need to dis­ cover what pleases, and what displeases, their gods. They believed that

those gods had more arete, time, and strength than mankind, or in other words that they excelled in just those qualities in which mortal aristocrats outshone human kakoi. It seems reasonable to infer that their gods were motivated by similar considerations; and reason­ able or not, it is the inference that they in fact drew. Most divine behavior in Homer can be illuminated by a comparison with the behavior of human aristocrats, rather than the behavior of disinter­ ested judges. The gods are respecters of persons. The Cyclops Polyphemos had behaved in a manner shocking to Greek standards of hospitality and civilized behavior. But he was Poseidon’s son: he had only to pray to his father and Poseidon persecuted Odysseus, regardless of justice. Similarly, it was not for the justice of Achilles’ case, or indeed for any claim that he possessed, that Zeus saw to it that the Greeks fared badly as long as Agamemon had not placated Achilles: it was a favor that Zeus owed to Achilles’ mother. It was the blood- relationship between Thetis and Achilles that made the favor avail­ able for Achilles. Moreover, it was a favor that Zeus did not wish to grant; and here again we encounter the Greek gods as immortal aristocrats. Zeus is afraid of the dissension that will ensue between Hera and himself if he helps the Trojans, whom he favors anyway, since they have always sacrificed to him abundantly. The dissension begins; and Hephaistos says ‘this is a bad thing and passes what can be endured, if you two quarrel in this manner for the sake of mortals . .. Conclusion From our discussions it has become apparent that Homeric values frequently do not achieve the goals of Homeric society. They do not ensure that the interests of a larger good and a larger group than the oikos may be taken into account, on the—apparently rare— occasions when these are relevant. The kings are endowed with a great deal of time to ensure that they will fight in the forefront of the battle on behalf of all; but it is as individuals in command of their oikoi or contingents that they possess their time and prestige. In Iliad 1, Nestor attempts to mediate by pointing out to Achilles and Agamemnon that only the Trojans will benefit from their quarrel. Neither is incapable of understanding Nestor’s point, but each is afraid of being put in a bad light, competitively speaking, by the other, of being spoken of as ‘a mere nobody.’ In Iliad 1, Agamemnon has two goals. He wishes to take Briseis there is a word for ‘just’ in Homeric Greek, and Homer does not use it in such contexts as these. 712 A. W. H. to defend itself. The suitors have committed atasthalicd against Odysseus and his oikos; yet to kill them must harm Ithaca much more than their misdeeds have done. Furthermore, since both parties would be in a very aäscktm condition were they not to fight, there seems to be no alternative to another battle, in which, says Homer, the party of Odysseus would have killed all the families of the suitors, had not Athena appeared and administered oaths to both sides. It is some­ what surprising that so many scholars find Achilles’ situation more ethically complex than that of Odysseus, whose situation they hardly discuss at all. Both Achilles and Odysseus are saying that nothing could possibly be enough; and Odysseus knows (a) that agathoi are so termed because they make both their own oikos and their polis more able to defend itself and (b) that he and his allies have made Ithaka less capable of defending itself. Nothing can be done about the situ­ ation: the men are dead. But the comment of the aged Laertes, rejoicing that his son and his grandson are vying with one another in a contest of arete, may remind the audience that in killing over a hundred suitors Odysseus and his allies have been displaying arete. Nor are the values of the Trojans more successfully related to their goals. Troy is to be destroyed, but not while Hector lives. At the beginning of Iliad 22, the majority of the Trojan army has escaped in full rout back into Troy, leaving Hector outside the gates. It is vital, if the Trojans are to live to fight another day, that Hector retreat within the walls. On the batdements, Priam tears his hair, Hecuba bares her breasts, to no avail. Hector is unmoved. What moves him is the thought of Polydamas criticising his (Hector’s) ill- fated strategy. Rather than face such criticism he stays outside the Trojan wall, meets Achilles in combat, and is killed. Once again, the individualistic aspect of the arete-standard produces effects quite other than the goals aimed at by those who subscribed to the values. These problems are not moral, of a kind to be solved by living up to the values of one’s community. They are caused by the values themselves, and their solution calls for a kind of thought not to be expected from an epic poet Plato was still trying to
